math-k2.verdict:
No wrong answer keys found, but this should not ship as is. Two blockers and nine major issues need fixing first, and some of them hit K–1 children directly.

What checked out, using my own independent solvers over 58,400 items (every skill, level and locale, 400 seeds each):
- Every key matched my own answer.
- check() accepts every key and rejects every wrong choice and every listed wrong value.
- Choices are distinct, the key appears exactly once, and every wrong choice has a kebab-case why tag.
- No hint or step shows a false equation.
- No `say` line contains ^, digit/digit or braces.
- Spanish is present everywhere; the only string identical to English is "Piano".

The blockers:
- Fraction-bar items that say "Cut the bar into fourths/thirds/halves" are marked correct without cutting. One tap on the uncut bar sends "1/1". Shading 2/4 for "one half", or 4/4 for "three thirds", is also accepted.
- The "Left/Right" and "Left to right: cats, dogs, fish" questions break on phones. On the integration branch (`foundation`) the tap-to-mark counters wrap groups onto new lines. At 320–430 px, 65–89% of m.compare.groups items and 100% of m.data.picture items stack the groups vertically. About 48% of m.data.picture items also stack on desktop.

The author's report is mostly accurate, with these corrections:
- The fraction-by-value note understates the problem (see the first blocker).
- The coin note understates it: the swap tag is wrong in English too.
- "Avoided '2 thirds'" is not true; m.shares.thirds L2 uses "2 thirds", "3 fourths" and "3 halves" as wrong choices. These are fine for 2.G.A.3, but the note is wrong.

Nothing was committed. All throwaway audit files are deleted, and the worktree is clean at b813cea.

findings.where: apps/web/src/practice/math/k2-more.ts — m.shares.halves L2 (lines ~1366-1415) and m.shares.thirds L1 (lines ~2412-2440), both locales
findings.problem:
The answer is {kind:'fraction'} checked by value, and the pad has no fixed parts. The foundation FractionBarPad starts as 1 uncut part, so one tap sends "1/1".

"1/1" is accepted for every whole-bar item: 222/800 m.shares.halves L2 items and 270/800 m.shares.thirds L1 items. Example: "Cut the bar into fourths. Shade all 4 fourths." A child who never cuts is marked right.

The same check also accepts 2/4 for "Cut the bar into halves. Shade one half." It accepts 2/2 or 3/3 for "Cut into thirds/fourths, shade all" (728 and 652 such cases across these levels). So partitioning, the point of 1.G.A.3 and 2.G.A.3, is never checked, and wrong work is recorded as correct.
findings.fix: For any 'Cut the bar into X' item, require the exact response. Either use answer {kind:'text', accept:[`${n}/${d}`]} (norm() keeps digits and '/', so '1/1' and '2/4' fail), or add an exact-parts flag to fraction answers. Add wrong values ['1/1','did-not-cut'] and equivalent cuts (e.g. ['2/4','made-fourths-not-halves']). Alternatively fix the parts with pad.parts and reword to 'The bar has d parts'.

findings.where: k2-more.ts m.compare.groups L1-3 (lines ~609-659) and m.data.picture L1-3 (lines ~1184-1285), en+es, with markable:true rendered by foundation MarkCounters
findings.problem:
These questions depend on the groups sitting side by side: choices 'Left / Right / Same', the legend 'Left to right: cats, dogs, fish', the hint 'It is group number 2 from the left', and alt 'one on the left and one on the right'.

Markable dots are drawn by MarkCounters, which wraps groups onto new lines at 56 px K–2 cells. Measured with the same layout algorithm:
- m.compare.groups stacks top/bottom in 355/400 items at a 320 px phone, 322/400 at 375 px and 260/400 at 430 px.
- m.data.picture stacks in 400/400 items on every phone and about 194/400 at desktop width (654 px).

A kindergartener asked 'left or right?' about two stacked groups has no correct answer to find, and the legend order no longer matches what is drawn.
findings.fix: Draw a label under each group and refer to the label instead of position: 'A'/'B', or the category icon/name for data.picture. Choices become the labels (e.g. 🐱 Cats). Remove 'Left to right' and 'group number N from the left'. Alternatively give comparison dots a layout that never wraps (shrink cells as arrays do), and add a test that runs layoutCounters at 286 px.

findings.where: k2-more.ts STORY_100 take-add (lines 177-178) and generator case 'take-add' (line ~1486), m.story.100 L3, en+es
findings.problem:
c is drawn from 5..min(40, 99-(a-b)) with no tie to b. In 456 of 982 take-add items (46%), more books or sheep come back than ever left.

Example: 'There are 35 sheep in a field. Then 18 go into the barn. Later 32 come back out.' Another: 'Kids borrow 5. Then 40 come back.' The arithmetic key is right, but the story is impossible, and a careful child will doubt the problem.
findings.fix: Draw c = r.int(Math.min(5, b), b) (or c ≤ b) for take-add, keeping a - b + c ≤ 99. Add a test that the number coming back is at most the number that left.

findings.where: k2-more.ts m.money.count L3 'Which coins make X¢?' (lines ~2104-2131), English
findings.problem:
The 'swapped-nickel-and-dime' option is made by swapping one dime for one nickel. Nobody who mixes up nickel and dime values would pick that set.

Over 1,657 items with dimes or nickels:
- In 1,183 (71%), the swap-tagged option does not total the target if a dime is worth 5¢ and a nickel 10¢.
- In 242, the option that child would pick carries a different tag. Example: 'Which coins make 11¢?' — the swapper picks '1 nickel and 1 penny', which is tagged counted-one-too-few.

So the learner model records the wrong misconception.
findings.fix: Build the swap distractor as the purse that equals the target under swapped values (nickel=10, dime=5), and tag only that option 'swapped-nickel-and-dime'. Give other wrong sets a generic tag such as 'miscounted-the-set'. Add a test that re-values each tagged option with swapped values.

findings.where: k2-more.ts m.money.count L1-3 Spanish (QUARTER/DIME/NICKEL/PENNY .es and coinsEs, lines ~360-376, 2151-2161)
findings.problem:
Spanish prompts write each coin's value ('estas monedas: 3 de 10¢, 2 de 5¢'). The Spanish skill is therefore plain repeated addition and never tests knowing coin values (2.MD.C.8). English learners must recall that a dime is 10¢.

Spanish items still emit 'swapped-nickel-and-dime' wrong values (e.g. 10[swapped-nickel-and-dime] for '1 de 10¢ y 5 de 1¢') and L3 swap tags. That error cannot happen when the value is printed, so the tag adds noise to Spanish learners' records. The author noted this but left the tags in.
findings.fix: Show coin pictures without values in both languages, or use US-Spanish coin names ('una moneda de diez centavos (dime)') consistently. At minimum, drop the swap tags in 'es', and mark the Spanish item as value-given so the two languages are not counted as the same evidence.

findings.where: k2-more.ts m.measure.units L1 (lines ~1054-1074); same pattern in m.measure.ruler L1-2 (lines ~2290-2324)
findings.problem:
'How many cubes long is the ribbon?' draws {kind:'array', rows:1, cols:n}. ArrayVisual and MarkCounters draw that as a row of separate round dots with gaps between them, not as touching cubes, and it is not attached to the 🎀 emoji above.

This contradicts the L3 lesson in the same skill ('Units must touch, with no gaps') and the prompt word 'cubes'. The alt text ('A ribbon with cubes lined up along it, end to end') describes a picture that is not drawn.

The ruler items have the same gap: the object is never drawn on the ruler, yet the alt says 'A carrot lies on it'. At L2 the start point exists only in text.
findings.fix: Add a measuring visual: the object as a bar with touching unit squares (or ruler ticks) under it, starting at its real start. Until then, rewrite the alt to say what is drawn and avoid calling separate dots cubes. For the ruler, draw the object segment from s to end.

findings.where: k2-more.ts m.measure.ruler L3 compare (lines ~2236-2261), en+es say
findings.problem:
`say` is the same as the prompt and uses abbreviations: 'A green string is 20 in long. A red string is 7 in long.' Text-to-speech reads 'twenty in long'. Spanish says 'mide 20 pulg', and TTS reads 'pulg'. Some engines also read 'cm' as the letters.

K–2 learners depend on read-aloud. The printed '20 in long' is also confusing for a second grader, and the Spanish abbreviation is 'pulg.' with a period.
findings.fix: Use full unit words in the sentence and in say ('20 inches long', '20 pulgadas', '34 centímetros'). Keep the abbreviation only after the answer blank, written as 'pulg.' in Spanish. Add a check that say has no unit abbreviations.

findings.where: k2-more.ts m.count.100 L1; m.shares.halves L1-3; m.shares.thirds L1-2; m.teen.numbers L1-2; m.write.20 L1-2 (both locales)
findings.problem:
The item pools are tiny. Distinct prompt+picture per level:
- m.count.100 L1: 7 (blank always last; decades 10–40 … 70–100 only)
- m.shares.halves L1: 5 (Spanish 4, because 'fourth' and 'quarter' both become 'cuarto'); L2: 6 (es 4); L3: 8
- m.shares.thirds L1: 6; L2: 6
- m.teen.numbers L1/L2: 9
- m.write.20 L2: 10

A practice set repeats items, and a child can pass by memory. This misses the brief's minimum of 12 distinct items per level.
findings.fix:
- m.count.100 L1: vary the blank position (at = r.int(0,3)), start from 0, and add counting back by tens.
- Shares: vary the shape (bars, rectangles, circles), contexts, and question type ('which bar shows thirds', 'is this cut into equal shares?'). Grade 2 can add 'two thirds' and 'three fourths' (allowed by 2.G.A.3).
- Add a test asserting at least 12 distinct items per level.

findings.where: k2-more.ts m.measure.units L2 (lines ~1075-1105), en+es
findings.problem: Lengths are random 6..15 vs 2..a-2, whatever the object. In 944 of 4,000 items (24%), a clearly shorter real object is stated to be the longer one in the same cubes. Examples: 'The key is 13 cubes long. The spoon is 4 cubes long.'; 'The caterpillar is 14 cubes long. The ribbon is 3 cubes long.'; 'The crayon is 9 cubes long. The pencil is 3 cubes long.' A demanding teacher would reject these.
findings.fix: Draw each length from the object's own range (THINGS already has inch ranges), and pick A and B so A is plausibly the longer one.

findings.where: k2-more.ts m.decompose.10 L1 hint 1 (line 721), en+es
findings.problem: When the first part is 1, the hint reads '10 dots in all. 1 are in the first group.' and in Spanish '1 están en el primer grupo.' This happens in 948 of 4,000 L1 items (24%).
findings.fix: Use singular forms when a === 1: '1 is in the first group' / '1 está en el primer grupo'.

findings.where: k2-more.ts m.decompose.10 L2 cands (line 731)
findings.problem: In 798 of 4,000 items (20%), two wrong choices are the same pair in swapped order. Example: '10 + 1' [used-the-total-as-a-part] and '1 + 10' [sum-too-big] (when a=1). A child who knows addition can be done in any order sees a duplicate, so the item really has 3 options.
findings.fix: Remove duplicate choices by sorted pair before calling choose(). When a = 1, use [a+1, b] or [a+2, b-1] for the 'sum-too-big' option.

findings.where: k2-more.ts m.place.1000 L3 'Which words name N?' (lines ~1675-1696)
findings.problem: When the tens and ones digits are equal and there is no teen or zero, only the wrong-hundreds distractor exists. Example: 'Which words name 377?' offers only 'three hundred seventy-seven' and 'four hundred seventy-seven', a 50/50 guess. This is 106 of 1,974 word-choice items (5%).
findings.fix: Always fill to 3 or 4 choices: add the tens off by one ('three hundred sixty-seven') or the 'wrote-each-part' reading.

findings.where: k2-more.ts m.time.set L1 and L3 o'clock items with h = 12 (line ~1157)
findings.problem: The foundation ClockPad starts at 12:00 and sends that time if untouched. 'Show 12 o'clock' is therefore right without moving the hands: about 8% of L1 items and 522 of 12,000 items overall.
findings.fix: Leave out h = 12 for o'clock items, or have the pad start at a different time for them.

findings.where: k2-more.ts Spanish copy: m.time.set/m.time.5min hints (lines 1173, 2214); m.measure.units L3 labels (lines 1115-1117); m.data.picture steps (line 1243); m.data.chart question/hints (lines 2352-2385); m.count.100 hint (line 507); m.story.100 'fewer' nudge (line 1519)
findings.problem:
Several Spanish lines are unnatural or ungrammatical:
- 'Para y media, la manecilla larga apunta al 6.' / 'Para en punto, …'
- 'Muy grande' / 'Muy pequeña' used for 'too big / too small' (muy = very)
- 'Bloques tuvo más votos.' / 'Galletas saladas tuvo más votos.' (plural subject, singular verb)
- '¿…para manzanas y peras juntos?' (feminine nouns)
- 'Luego quita saltar la cuerda.'
- 'las decenas suben uno'
- 'Menos quiere decir menos que 62.' (circular)
findings.fix:
- 'Para la media hora, la manecilla larga apunta al 6.' / 'Para la hora en punto, …'
- 'Demasiado grande' / 'Demasiado pequeña' (or 'sale más grande de lo que es')
- 'Los bloques tuvieron más votos.'
- '…para manzanas y peras, sumadas?'
- 'Luego quita los votos de saltar la cuerda.'
- 'las decenas aumentan en uno'
- 'Menos quiere decir que sembró menos que 62.'

findings.where: k2-more.ts alt texts: m.measure.units L2 (line 1089), m.measure.ruler L1-2 (line 2303), m.decompose.10 L1 (line 717), m.money.count (lines 2122, 2154)
findings.problem:
Several alt texts describe something that is not drawn:
- 'A ribbon and a carrot' when only 🎀 is shown.
- 'A carrot lies on it and ends at a dot' when the line has only a dot.
- 'Two groups of dots side by side' when they stack on phones (73% at 320 px).
- 'Coins' for the 💰 money-bag emoji.
findings.fix: Describe exactly what is rendered, e.g. 'A ribbon', 'A ruler from 0 to 15 cm with a dot at the end', 'Two groups of dots', 'A money bag'.

findings.where: k2-more.ts why tags: m.story.10 L3 (line 783), m.odd.even L1 (lines 1819/1858), m.count.100 L2 (via numberChoices filler, line 48), m.write.20 L2 n=20 (line 587)
findings.problem:
Some why tags describe a mistake the child could not have made at that level:
- 'counted-crossed-out' at L3, where no dots are crossed out.
- 'looked-at-the-tens-digit' on a dot picture with no digits.
- 99 tagged 'off-by-one' for the blank after 97, 98, 99 (it is the number already on screen, i.e. repeated-last-number).
- 10 tagged 'counted-empty-boxes' for two full frames (20), where there are no empty boxes.

These wrong tags reach the learner model.
findings.fix: Make tags depend on the level and picture: e.g. 'gave-the-part-taken' at L3, 'mixed-up-odd-and-even' for dot pictures, 'repeated-last-number' for values already shown. Drop counted-empty-boxes when no box is empty.

findings.where: k2-more.ts hints: m.decompose.10 L1 hint 2 (line 722); m.shares.halves L3 and m.shares.thirds L3 compare hint 2 (lines 1339, 2500); m.story.100 change-take hint 3 via tensFirst (rare)
findings.problem:
Some hints give the answer away:
- 'Count the dots in the second group.' — the second group is the missing part.
- 'More equal parts means smaller parts.' — states the answer to 'which share is smaller'.
- In rare change-take items, hint 3 is the story equation itself, e.g. '67 − 30 = 37' for 'had 67, now 37 left, how many sold?' (answer 30).
findings.fix:
- decompose: hint 'Count on from a to n'.
- compare: hint 'Picture each bar cut up. Which pieces look bigger?'
- tensFirst: when the hint's result equals a number in the story, use the count-back hint instead.

findings.where: k2-more.ts m.time.5min L1-2 wrong lists (line 2211)
findings.problem: Some items list no likely wrong answers (14/800 at L1, 38/800 at L2), e.g. 'Show 4:20' and '25 minutes after 5'. The swapped-hands value equals the key, and the other tags only fire for :05, :10 or minutes of 30 and above. Those misses go unrecorded.
findings.fix: Always add at least one tagged wrong value, e.g. hh(h, m/5) ['wrote-the-number-pointed-at'] or hh(next, m) ['used-the-next-hour'] for every m.

findings.where: k2-more.ts standard codes: m.data.chart (2.MD.D.10), m.data.picture (1.MD.C.4), m.measure.ruler L3, m.place.1000 L2-3
findings.problem:
- m.data.chart claims 2.MD.D.10 (bar graphs) but shows a text table, and m.data.picture's picture graph is unlabelled dot groups (author flagged both).
- m.measure.ruler L3 tests 2.MD.A.2 and 2.MD.A.4, not A.1.
- m.place.1000 L2/L3 (expanded form, number names) is 2.NBT.A.3.

Reports will overstate what is covered.
findings.fix: Add a bar-graph visual before claiming 2.MD.D.10. Otherwise retitle and recode: list the extra standards, or split the skills.

math-35.verdict: No wrong answer keys found. Every key in all 24 skills (64 levels) matched my own independent solver over 400 seeds per level in both locales. I also checked that the solvers would catch a bad key: a changed key was caught 200/200 times at every level. The checker accepts every key, rejects every wrong choice and every listed wrong value, and every wrong choice carries a kebab-case why tag. English and Spanish always carry the same key and the same numbers, no English leaks into the Spanish, and every level has at least 12 distinct items (the smallest are symmetry L2 with 13 and fraction-bar L1 with 16). It is not ready to ship as is, because of content problems the key checks cannot see: (1) about 8% of the perimeter polygons cannot exist (sides like 15, 3, 3); (2) in m.frac.equiv.model L1 (77% of items), m.mult.compare L3 (35%) and m.div.2digit L1 (45%) the third hint states the final answer; (3) the clock-angle hint, followed literally, makes a child call 3:00 and 9:00 acute; (4) the bar-graph L2 and line-plot skills never show a graph or plot, and the line-plot hint tells the child to count Xs that are not there; (5) one Spanish hint ("cuántos niños hay en la clase") reads as "how many boys". On top of these there are Spanish and English grammar slips and some unrealistic numbers. The symmetry draft facts are all correct. The author's notes held up: the merged standard codes, the missing pictures, the touch-pad contract (it matches the pads on the foundation branch) and the real-world numbers are all as stated.
math-35.sampled: Setup: worktree reset to 8d019e5 and node_modules cloned. I read all 4119 lines of apps/web/src/practice/math/g3to5-more.ts. I wrote a throwaway vitest harness, now deleted and never committed. It runs all 24 skills, every level, en and es, at 400 seeds each: 25,600 seed/level pairs and 51,200 items. Checks: (1) the key re-derived from the English prompt, visual and pad by my own solvers (column arithmetic, integer thousandths, clock minutes, cross-multiplying, my own unit-factor tables and symmetry-count table), plus a check that a changed key gets caught; (2) check(answer, answerText(answer)) accepts the key and rejects every wrong choice and listed wrong value; (3) choices distinct, the key present exactly once, why tags on wrong choices; (4) hints that contain the answer, separating real giveaways from coincidences and cases where the answer is already in the prompt; (5) notation in say; (6) Spanish present, different from English, no English words; (7) alt text that gives the answer away; (8) distinct items per level. I also checked the touch-pad steps and ranges, the keypad keys, polygon side lengths, and grammar patterns. The author's g3to5-more.test.ts and skills.test.ts pass (398 tests). I read 5-7 items per skill-level in both languages in full (about 350 bilingual items), not 25 per skill; patterns found there were then counted over all 400 seeds. I checked AnswerPad.tsx and the foundation branch's pad-math, FractionBarPad, ClockPad and answer.ts for the touch-pad contract.

findings.where: apps/web/src/practice/math/g3to5-more.ts:1992 and :2053, m.perimeter.missing L1 (listed sides) and L2 (missing last side), en+es
findings.problem: Side lengths are drawn independently from 2-15, so some polygons cannot exist. Examples: 'A goat pen is shaped like a triangle. Its sides are 15 ft, 3 ft and 3 ft'; 'Its sides are 5 m, 9 m and 4 m' (a flat triangle); L2 'perimeter 18 m, two sides 5 m and 9 m' gives a last side of 4. This affects 19/235 L1 and 15/198 L2 polygon items (about 8%). A teacher would mark the problem as false.
findings.fix: Redraw until the longest side is less than the sum of the other sides (strictly). For L2, apply the same rule to the full side list, including the hidden last side.

findings.where: g3to5-more.ts:1823 (hint 3) with PAIRS3 at :394, m.frac.equiv.model L1, en+es
findings.problem: Hint 3 is the unit equivalence '1/p = k/q' (or 'k/p = 1/q'). Whenever s=1 or n=1 this is exactly the answer: 'The bar shows 1/2. Shade ... eighths' gets hint 3 '1/2 = 4/8.'; '3/6 → halves' gets '3/6 = 1/2.'. Three of the five pairs use halves, so this happens in 309/400 items, and the level has only 16 distinct items.
findings.fix: When s=1 or n=1, make hint 3 a partial step, e.g. 'Split each half into 4 equal pieces. How many pieces are shaded now?'. Add more pairs (3→6, 4→8 with s>1, 2→4 with 2/4→?/8) so halves are not most of the items.

findings.where: g3to5-more.ts:2686, m.mult.compare L3 (remainder stories without `first`: modes down/left), en+es
findings.problem: Hint 3 is the full division '71 ÷ 6 = 11 R 5.'. For 'How many cookies are left over?' and 'How many full rows?' the answer is the remainder or the quotient written in that hint, and hint 2 has just said 'so the answer is the remainder'. 141/400 items give the answer away.
findings.fix: Make hint 3 a partial step, e.g. 'How many 6s fit in 71? 6 × 11 = 66.', so the child still has to find the remainder and decide what it means.

findings.where: g3to5-more.ts:3106, m.angles L1 (clock form), en+es
findings.problem: 'Count the hour marks between the hands and multiply by 30°' gives the wrong count. At 3:00 or 9:00 the marks strictly between the hands are 2, which gives 60°, so a child following the hint picks 'acute' when the answer is right. At 4:00 or 8:00 it gives 90° ('right') when the angle is obtuse, and at 1:00 it gives 0°. Hint 3 then says the hands are '3 hour marks apart', which contradicts it. This affects 149/400 items. The L1 question also does not say 'smaller angle' (L2 does).
findings.fix: Use 'Count the jumps from one number to the next, going the short way from one hand to the other, and multiply by 30°' (Spanish: 'Cuenta los saltos de un número al siguiente…'). Add 'the smaller angle' to the L1 question at :3094.

findings.where: g3to5-more.ts:2361-2416, m.bargraph.scaled L2 (all items)
findings.problem: The 'bar graph' exists only as sentences ('The bar for flute ends halfway between 6 and 8'). No graph is shown, so the skill of reading a scaled bar graph (3.MD.B.3) is never practised at this level. The child is only translating text.
findings.fix: Add a bar-graph Visual (bars, scale lines, labels) and drop the sentence descriptions, or retitle the level as word problems and mark the gap in the skill status.

findings.where: g3to5-more.ts:3695-3696 and hint at :3719, m.lineplot.frac L1/L2
findings.problem: No line plot is ever shown: the data come as a list, and the visual is an empty number line from 0 to 1 that cannot be marked (no `markable`). The L1 count hint says 'Count the Xs above that number', but there are no Xs. The 5.MD.B.2 skill 'line plots with fractions' is not what the child actually does.
findings.fix: Draw the line plot (stacked Xs above eighths) from `data`, or make the number line markable so the child builds the plot. Until then, change the hint to 'Count each 3/8 in the list.'

findings.where: g3to5-more.ts:364, m.multdiv.word L3 gym-class story, es
findings.problem: The story says '6 niñas y 15 niños', then the Spanish hint says 'Primero encuentra cuántos niños hay en la clase'. Next to 'niñas', 'niños' reads as 'boys', so the hint points to 15 rather than the total of 21. This affects 37/400 Spanish L3 items.
findings.fix: Use 'cuántos estudiantes hay en total en la clase' (and in the English, 'how many students in all').

findings.where: g3to5-more.ts:3298 (L1 hint 3), :3341 (L3 hint 3 = lines[0]), m.div.2digit
findings.problem: L1: hint 3 'R × est = …, so try est' names the answer whenever the estimate is already right (180/400). L3: when the quotient has one digit (q 5-9), the first long-division stage is the whole answer, e.g. '217 ÷ 26 = 8, with 9 left over.' (20/400). Also, 7/400 L1 worked steps jump by 2 ('17 × 7 = 119, which is too little, so try 9') without checking 8.
findings.fix: L1: end hint 3 at the estimate product ('60 × 4 = 240. Now multiply 61 by your estimate.'). L3: for single-stage items, give 'How many 26s fit in 217? Start with 26 × 8.'. In steps, adjust one step at a time.

findings.where: apps/web/src/components/practice/AnswerPad.tsx:273-288 at 8d019e5; affects m.frac.equiv.model L1 (fraction-bar), m.time.elapsed L1 and L3 (clock), m.dec.thousandths L2 and m.frac.asdiv L3 (number-line)
findings.problem: At this commit, AnswerInput has no cases for 'number-line', 'fraction-bar' or 'clock', so these 5 levels cannot be answered on this branch alone. The pads exist on `foundation` (0fc9d0d), and their contracts match the author's assumptions: 'h:mm', decimal responses from min/max/step, fixed `parts`.
findings.fix: Merge only into `foundation`, which has the touch pads, then run one Runner test per pad on these five levels.

findings.where: g3to5-more.ts:3877 (say) and :3883 (hint 2), m.convert.multistep L2 'and a half' items
findings.problem: Spanish says '¿1 galones y medio…', '¿1 pies y medio…', '¿1 minutos y medio…' when w=1 (20/400 Spanish items). The English hint says 'half of a hour is 30 minutes' (15/400).
findings.fix: Use uName(c.big, w, locale) for the count, so w=1 gives 'galón'/'pie'. Write 'half an hour' (or use an article helper).

findings.where: text.ts sayFrac used at g3to5-more.ts:773-808 (FRAC_TIMES_STORIES sayEs), :1876 (pizza story), :3152 (angles L2), :3691 (line plot), es
findings.problem: The read-aloud says 'un medio de hora', 'un medio de taza', 'comió un medio de una pizza', 'un medio de una vuelta completa', 'miden un medio de pie'. eng-grammar-35.verdict: Not ready to ship as is. Every item is well formed: across 400 seeds, every skill, every level and both languages, every key checks, no wrong choice is accepted, tags and say text are clean, and the computed dictionary-order skill matches an independent collator. But four item groups (about 11 items) mark a correct answer wrong. Several hints also give the answer away or point the child to the wrong choice. All fixes are small, local edits to the banks or hint strings in apps/web/src/practice/english/grammar-35.ts.
eng-grammar-35.sampled:
Reset the worktree to cae69b3 and cloned node_modules. Wrote throwaway vitest audits (deleted afterwards; git status is clean, nothing committed). They ran all 26 skills, every level, both locales and 400 seeds each (0-299 plus 100 spread seeds), about 41,000 items.

Checks:
- Choices are distinct and the key appears exactly once.
- Exactly one choice lacks a why tag, and every tag is well-formed kebab-case.
- check(answer, keyIndex) is correct and every other index is rejected. answerText returns the key label. Note: check(answer, answerText(...)) is false for every choice item by design, because the checker compares indices; Runner and tools.ts pass the index.
- Hint text scanned for the key, and hint 3 scanned for naming every wrong choice.
- say has no ^, digit/digit, braces or ___; no undefined/NaN/spacing junk in any text.
- English and Spanish differ and the slot pairing is consistent.
- No visuals or alt text exist.
- Each level has at least 12 distinct items in both rendered output and banks.

Independent re-derivation of keys:
- Dictionary order, both levels and both languages, by Intl.Collator('en'/'es'): ñ after n; ch and ll as two letters. 0 mismatches.
- My own rules and tables for EN plurals, ES plurals, EN possessives, EN comparatives, EN and ES perfect tenses, EN progressive, EN/ES title capitalisation, and EN quote / ES raya dialogue patterns. 0 mismatches, apart from one parse failure on my side (dogs', checked by hand).

Read every bank entry in the 2,904-line source in both languages as a teacher and a native Spanish speaker. Also read rendered samples (about 25 per level, both languages, with generated hints and worked lines). Checked the author's report claims; the author's test and skills.test pass (478 tests).

findings.where: apps/web/src/practice/english/grammar-35.ts e.verb.tenses level 2, es, ES_TIME lines 472, 475, 478, 481, 483 (English counterparts at 454, 457, 460, 463, 465 are weaker)
findings.problem: On all 5 items keyed to the future, the present form is a wrong choice tagged present-for-future: cruzan, viaja, limpia, presenta, prepara. But present tense with a future time word is standard Spanish (RAE's "presente prospectivo": "Mañana salgo para Lima"). "Mañana mamá prepara panqueques" and "En dos semanas nuestra clase presenta una obra de teatro" are correct, so a child who picks them is marked wrong and gets a false misconception tag. The question "Elige el verbo que va con el tiempo" does not rule the present out. English has the same issue on a smaller scale: "In two weeks our class performs a play" is acceptable English for a scheduled event.
findings.fix: In the Spanish future-keyed items, replace the present choice with a form that is really wrong (for example the imperfect: cruzaban, viajaba, limpiaba) and keep the preterite, or change the question to "¿Qué forma está en futuro simple?". In English, either drop the present choice from the scheduled-event items ("In two weeks…", "Tomorrow Mom…") or use time words that rule out a timetable reading.

findings.where: grammar-35.ts e.comparatives level 2, es, line 601
findings.problem: "Sofía tiene cinco años. Es la ___ de las tres hermanas." is keyed "menor", with "mayor" tagged reversed-comparison. The sentence never gives the other sisters' ages, so "mayor" fits the text just as well. Hint 3 ("Sofía es la que tiene menos años de las tres") claims a fact the text does not give. The item cannot be answered as written.
findings.fix: "Sofía tiene cinco años, y sus hermanas tienen ocho y diez. Es la ___ de las tres."

findings.where: grammar-35.ts e.possessives level 1, en, lines 311, 317, 319; level 2, en, line 337
findings.problem:
The possessive of the other number is offered as wrong, but it is grammatical and natural, and nothing in the sentence fixes how many owners there are (only hint 3 says so):
- "The trees' leaves turned orange." (wrong choice: trees')
- "The birds' nest was high in the oak tree." (a pair of birds shares a nest)
- "The lions' roar echoed across the zoo."
- Level 2: "The twin's room has two beds." (wrong choice: twin's)
A child who writes any of these correct sentences is marked wrong.
findings.fix: Put the number of owners in the sentence: "That one ___ leaves turned orange", "One little ___ nest…", "The big ___ roar…" (with an article that only works for one), and "The two ___ room has two beds". Or switch to nouns where a second owner is implausible.

findings.where: grammar-35.ts e.tense.shifts level 1, en line 2198 and es line 2214

findings.where: grammar-35.ts e.comparatives level 2, es, line 600
findings.problem: "Mis abuelos son las personas ___ de la familia." is keyed "mayores", with "más mayores" tagged doubled-comparison. The wrong choice can be defended.
findings.fix: "Mi abuelo tiene 80 años. Es el ___ de la familia." with choices mayor / más mayor / menor, where "el más mayor" is clearly wrong.

findings.where: grammar-35.ts e.progressive.tenses, es, hint 2 line 1314; affects items at lines 1293, 1297, 1305

eng-reading-35.verdict: No wrong answer keys found. I recomputed every key independently in both languages, including the narrator key from my own pronoun scan, and the checker, choices, tags, say text and Spanish coverage are all clean. The strand still should not ship as is, for five major reasons. (1) Grades 3–5 learners see the whole passage inside the centered, semibold h1 meant for one-line problems, so headings, boxes and glossaries look like every other line. That undercuts e.text.features. (2) About 65% of e.point.of.view items are the same two-option narrator question, so guessing goes a long way. (3) Pools of 13–19 entries per level mean a 10-item set repeats about 3 identical passage+question items, and about 58% of 5-item checks contain a repeat. (4) The launch-day poem asks "What is the poem mostly about?", and the plot-summary distractor is a defensible answer. (5) The science-fair story keys "both groups had the same conditions except for the music", but the text puts the 'silent' group on the same windowsill while music plays. There are also a handful of minor text-logic, Spanish-grammar and display slips. Facts checked against standard references are otherwise accurate.
eng-reading-35.sampled: Setup: reset to b42b852, cloned node_modules, author's tests pass (309). Wrote a throwaway vitest audit (since deleted; tree clean, nothing committed) that ran all 9 skills × 2 levels × 400 seeds × en/es (14,400 items). For each item it: traced the item back to its passage/question by text alone and compared the key with question.right. For narrator items it recomputed first/third person from its own scan of narration outside quotes. Results: 0 mismatches. check(answer,index) accepts only the key. check(answer, answerText(answer)) is false for every choice item in the product because check takes the index; this is platform behavior, not this strand. Choices are distinct after normalizing, the key appears exactly once, and every wrong choice has a valid tag. No hint contains the answer label, though hint 3 often nearly restates it (45 cases). I recomputed hint-2 locations (paragraph, stanza, section, box) in BOTH languages; the author only tested English: 0 errors. say has no notation and ends the prompt. No visuals or alt text. The key index is the same in both languages, Spanish differs from English in every field, and no English leaked into Spanish. 13–19 distinct items per level in each locale. Measured narrator share of the pov pool: 66% at L1, 64% at L2. Then read every passage and all 240 questions (214 on passages + 26 on pairs) in both languages, far beyond 25 per skill. Fact-checked bees, sea turtles, butter, moon phases, monarchs, seeds, basketball 1891–1936, hummingbirds, drums/steel pan, water cycle, Hawaii hot spot, camels, Wright brothers, coral, yeast/gluten, beavers, Braille, PET recycling and the ISS. Also read a sample of 72 fully rendered items (hints and worked steps), the Runner/MathText rendering, set and check sizing in learning/engine.ts, and the tutor check_answer tool.

findings.where: apps/web/src/practice/english/passages-35.ts:1343 (launch-day, e.story.theme L2, en+es)
findings.problem: The theme question is worded "What is the poem mostly about?" / "¿De qué trata principalmente el poema?". The distractor tagged plot-summary, "An aunt rides a rocket to the space station.", is a literally correct answer to that wording. The key, "Missing someone far away but still feeling close to her", is an inference: the poem never says the speaker misses her. So there are two defensible answers, and the child who picks the summary is marked wrong.
findings.fix: Reword to "What is the message of the poem?" / "¿Cuál es el mensaje del poema?". Make the key something the poem shows, such as "Even when someone you love is far away, you can still feel close to them." Keep the summary as the plot-summary distractor.

findings.where: apps/web/src/practice/english/passages-35.ts:741,745,759 (science-fair, e.key.details L2 "How did Lucía keep her test fair?", en+es)
findings.problem: Both plant groups sit on the same bedroom windowsill, yet one group is said to be left "in silence" while records play for the other every afternoon. The silent group hears the same music. The judge then praises the setup for using "the same window", and the key says she kept everything the same except the music. That models a broken control as careful science, in a story whose lesson is careful science.
findings.fix: Put the groups in two rooms with matching sunny windows ("one group on my windowsill, the other on the matching window in Mateo's room, with the door closed"). Change the judge's line to "the same amount of sun, the same water, and the same soil". Mirror both changes in the Spanish.

findings.where: apps/web/src/components/practice/Runner.tsx:209-211 rendering every ENGLISH_READING_3_5 item (worst for e.text.features and e.compare.texts)
findings.problem: The whole prompt (title, 5–9 paragraphs, and two texts for compare, up to about 480 words) is rendered inside the problem <h1>: centered, font-brand semibold, text-t2/sm:text-t1 (20/26px), line-height 1.15. Article headings, 'Fast fact' boxes, timelines and glossaries are plain centered lines that look like every other line. e.text.features asks "Under which heading…" about headings that do not look like headings. Screen readers get a 300-word h1, and "Text 1:"/"Text 2:" are not set apart.
findings.fix: Give reading items a passage block, either a structured prompt or a new `passage` field: left-aligned body text at normal weight and line-height, title and headings styled as headings, boxes and glossary styled as asides. Keep only the question in the h1. A minimal version is a `passage?: {title; blocks}` on ItemBody that Runner renders above the question.

findings.where: apps/web/src/practice/english/reading-35.ts:104,131 (e.point.of.view L1 and L2)
findings.problem: Every story adds the same two-option "Who is telling this story?" item with the same two labels. Measured over 400 seeds, that is 66% of L1 and 64% of L2 pov items. Guessing gets 50% on those items. Against the 5-item, pass-4 check, random guessing passes about 9.5% of the time, versus about 1.6% for four-choice items. Most pov practice is also one repeated question type.
findings.fix: Add a third and fourth option to the narrator item ("A character who tells it as 'we'", "An animal outside the story that speaks", "Two characters taking turns") or build it from real sentences, like bean-diary's "Which sentence shows…". Write more speaker and narrator questions so the narrator item is no more than a third of each pool, or include it for only half the stories.

findings.where: apps/web/src/practice/english/reading-35.ts:190 + learning/engine.ts buildPracticeSlots/buildCheckSlots (all 9 skills; pools 13–19 per level)
findings.problem: Each slot picks an entry independently, and nothing removes duplicates. With 13 entries, a 10-item practice set has a 99% chance of repeating an item and shows about 3 exact repeats on average (same 250-word passage, same question, choices reshuffled). A 5-item 'fresh' check repeats an item about 58% of the time. A repeated reading item costs 2–4 minutes, and a remembered answer counts toward readiness and checks.
findings.fix: For draft reading banks, remove duplicate slots by item text when building sets and checks: regenerate the seed until the pool entry is new, falling back to allowing repeats only when the pool is exhausted. Separately, grow each level to at least 25 entries before treating checks as evidence.

findings.where: passages-35.ts:634-635 (city-rain, en+es)
findings.problem: Stanza 5 has the rain stop ("When the clouds roll off at last, the sidewalks shine"), but the last stanza ends "tonight I fall asleep to the soft hum of the rain". The poem contradicts itself in a text children read closely.
findings.fix: End with something that still makes sound after the rain stops, for example "to the last drips from the roof" / "con las últimas gotas del techo".

findings.where: passages-35.ts:1033/1043 (camels, first sentence, en+es)

math-89.verdict: Not ready to ship. Every answer key is correct: I re-derived all 18 skills, every level, both locales, with my own evaluator, and found 0 mismatches. The problem is the answer pads. Two blockers stop a child who has the right answer from ever being marked correct. (1) On the fraction pad a whole-number key can never be entered. This hits about 60% of m.rate.change L1 items, including every rocket item, and about half of m.best.fit slope items. (2) m.irrational L3 asks for a number-line tap, but nothing in the app at this commit draws a number-line pad, so the question shows with no way to answer. One major issue: m.line.forms L1 marks the textbook answer "y = (3/2)x + 4" wrong and tells the child to "multiply it out". The rest are minor: weak or 2-choice distractors, zero tolerance on money and people, a few Spanish errors, and read-aloud and hint glitches. Everything the author claimed, I confirmed: tagged distractors, wrong values that are filtered, bilingual copy, prerequisites that resolve. Their own tests pass (367/367 together with skills.test).

math-67.verdict: Do not ship as is. The answer keys are right: my own solvers re-derived every key across all 19 skills, every level, both languages and 4,000 seeds per level, with 0 mismatches and 0 solver errors. But one blocker, two major issues and a set of minor ones stand. Blocker: on the fraction pad, any whole-number answer that must be in simplest form cannot be marked right (m.rational.multdiv L2 about 3.2% of items, m.rational.addsub L2 about 0.9% and L3 about 1.4%). Major: 64% of m.volume.frac L1 items have whole-number volumes that the fraction pad only accepts as "n/1". Major: on the foundation-branch number-line pad (not yet merged), m.rational.order L1 can be solved by matching the on-screen readout. Two of the author's own claims are also false: one tag is 41 characters, over their 40-character limit, and some typed items have no tagged wrong values. Nothing was committed and all scratch files are deleted.
math-67.sampled: Reset the worktree to 2856140 and cloned node_modules. Baseline: the author's g6to7-more.test.ts and skills.test.ts pass (385 tests). I wrote a throwaway harness in the worktree, now deleted, with independent solvers that read each prompt in both languages using my own phrase tables, exact rational arithmetic, brute force for inequalities, events and stories, and my own geometry and stats formulas. It ran every skill, level and locale at 300 seeds, then again at 4,000 seeds per level (about 400k items). It checked: (1) the key against my own result; (2) check() accepts answerText and rejects every wrong choice and listed wrong value; (3) choices are distinct, exactly one satisfies my solver and it is the keyed one, every wrong choice has a kebab-case tag of 40 characters or fewer, and the right choice has none; (4) whether any hint or (7) alt text contains the answer token, with each hit triaged by hand; (5) say contains no ^, digit/digit or braces, and none of − ≤ ≥ < > × ÷ % $ ° π; (6) English and Spanish both present, with Spanish prompts/say that are not copies of the English and no English words left in Spanish (or Spanish in English); (8) distinct items per level (all ≥ 26 once visuals are counted). It also checked that keys can be entered with the item's keys or pad, that number-line keys sit on the pad grid, that the read-aloud carries every number in the prompt, and that steps end on the key. Extra probes ran check() on typed variants (expanded form, pairs, n/1, "n/" and the π tolerance) and measured how often the realism problems occur. I read the foundation branch's FractionPad, NumberLinePad, pad-math, Runner and misconceptionOf to see how responses actually reach the checker. I read 25 sampled items per skill in English and Spanish (950 items, prompt, say, choices, hints, steps) as a teacher and a native Spanish reader. I also read the author's report (math-67.json) and verified its claims.

findings.where: g6to7-more.ts ratPlace lines 298-342 (m.rational.order L1, 100% of items), together with foundation's NumberLinePad.tsx and pad-math.ts
findings.problem: On the foundation pad, which matches the author's assumption, the placed point shows its value in a bubble and in the live region ("at −1.25"). I checked this by hand for the K, 4 and 7 bands at this commit, and it passes. Land the test change in the same merge as the courses.

findings.where: All 8 new course files, quiz scenes (rendered by components/stage/scenes.tsx QuizView, which never shuffles choices)
findings.problem: Answer-position bias. 73 of 100 quiz answers are choice 1. By file: figurative 12/13, figurativo-es 12/13, fact-opinion 11/14, rhymes 8/12, rimas-es 8/12, short-words 8/12, partes-es 8/12, parts-of-speech 6/12. A child who always taps the first choice scores 73% overall and 92% in the grade 4 courses. Retries are allowed, so the habit sticks. Existing courses (story-order, main-idea, fractions-es, matter) spread their answers across positions.
findings.fix: Rebalance answer positions in each file so that roughly a third sit at each index (and vary the yes/no items). Optionally also add a seeded shuffle of choices in QuizView, keyed by question id.

findings.where: english-short-words.ts lessons sound-it-out (s1, s2, q1, q3, alt text), short-vowels (sorter labels 'a, as in cat'), word-families (s1-s2 'op', q1 hint 'u, n', q2 'ig', q3 explanation 'op/ap', project 'ug'); also english-rhymes-syllables.ts clap-syllables s1 'ta, ble'
findings.problem: K-2 learners get a read-aloud button on every string, and speakText reads the raw text. 'Say the sounds slowly: c, a, t' comes out as 'see, ay, tee', and 'Blend the sounds s, u, n' comes out as 'ess, you, en'. Blending letter names never gives 'cat' or 'sun', so the core skill of the lesson is modelled wrongly. Word parts like 'ap', 'op', 'ig' and 'ug' get read as letters or abbreviations ('A.P.'). The author flagged this in the notes, but it is a teaching error, not just a wording choice.
findings.fix: Do not put isolated letters or word parts in spoken text. Describe sounds by keyword instead ('the first sound in cat, the middle sound you hear in apple, the last sound in hat'), or say whole words slowly ('Say cat very slowly. Hear three sounds?'). Longer term, add a say/audio field (the practice banks already have `say`) or recorded phoneme clips.

findings.where: english-parts-of-speech-es.ts lesson nouns: s2 'La prueba de el y la' ('“El feliz” no tiene sentido') and s6 q1 hint 'Prueba poner la o el antes de cada palabra' (choices lámpara / comer / alto)
findings.problem: The English 'the' test does not carry over to Spanish. Spanish readily turns infinitives and adjectives into nouns with an article. 'El comer' ('el comer bien es importante') and 'el alto' ('¿Cuál? —El alto') both make sense to a native speaker, so the q1 hint makes all three choices sound right. 'El feliz' is also usable as a noun phrase. The method the lesson teaches gives wrong results on its own quiz.
findings.fix: Replace the test with the meaning test the lesson already teaches ('¿Nombra una persona, animal, lugar o cosa?') plus a counting test ('dos lámparas' works; 'dos comer' does not). In q1, change the distractors to forms that cannot be read as nouns (e.g. 'come', 'muy'), and change the hint to match. Drop the 'El feliz' example.

findings.where: Titles and summaries of english-short-words.ts, english-rhymes-syllables.ts and english-rhymes-syllables-es.ts, as matched by catalogue/index.ts matchEntry (used on courses/new/[draftId] to say 'A ready-made course already covers this')
findings.problem: The new text adds generic words ('words', 'Reading', 'palabras') that the one-word matcher now hits. Results at 1464378: 'reading comprehension' (grade 4) gives 'Reading short words' (a grade 1 course); 'vocabulary words' (grade 3), 'sight words' (K) and 'spelling words' (grade 1) give 'Rhymes and syllables'; 'ortografía y palabras' (es) gives 'Rimas y sílabas'. At 55cfb79 all of these returned null, so a custom course was generated. The parent is now told, wrongly, that a course already covers the request, and one click enrols the child in it.
findings.fix: In matchEntry, skip generic words (word(s), palabra(s), reading/leer, learn/aprender, sentences/oraciones), and require either 2 or more hits or the same band as the learner. Or reword the summaries to avoid bare 'words'. Add the probes above as regression cases in catalogue.test.ts.

findings.where: english-rhymes-syllables-es.ts, english-parts-of-speech-es.ts, english-figurative-es.ts (subject: 'english') with i18n/es.ts 'subject.english': 'Inglés'; shown in courses/[courseId]/page.tsx:71, Landing.tsx:290, SchoolSection.tsx:55
findings.problem: These are the first Spanish-language reading and writing courses. The Spanish UI labels each one 'Inglés' (e.g. 'Inglés · Kínder' over 'Rimas y sílabas'), telling a parent the course teaches English when it teaches Spanish. The label is older than this commit, but these courses are the first to show it wrongly.
findings.fix: Make the subject label depend on the course language: subject 'english' with course locale 'es' shows 'Lengua' (or 'Lectura y escritura'), and keeps 'Inglés' for English-language courses. At minimum, decide on this before the Spanish courses ship.

findings.where: english-figurative.ts personification-hyperbole s2; english-figurative-es.ts personification-hyperbole s2
findings.problem: The list of feelings does not match the examples. EN: 'very busy, very annoyed, very tired' sits under 'million things to do / told you a thousand times / This bag weighs a ton', but the bag line means very heavy, not tired. ES: 'mucha hambre, mucho cansancio, mucha prisa' sits under 'Te lo he dicho mil veces / Me muero de hambre / Tengo tanta tarea…'; only hunger matches, and the first and third examples express annoyance and having too much to do.
findings.fix: EN: 'very busy, very annoyed, very heavy'. ES: 'mucha molestia, mucha hambre, muchísima tarea', in the same order as the examples.

findings.where: english-short-words.ts sound-it-out s1 'Each letter in a short word stands for a sound.'
findings.problem: Too broad, and the course's own words break it: fox (x = two sounds) in the same lesson's sorter, egg (gg = one sound) as the short-e key word in lesson 2, and 'the' and 'is' in lesson 4.
findings.fix: 'In words like cat, each letter stands for one sound.'

findings.where: english-rhymes-syllables.ts clap-syllables q1 hint ('Say piz-za'), q3 ('ti-ger'), rhyme-and-beat q3 ('rain-bow'); english-rhymes-syllables-es.ts q1 ('lu-na'), q3 ('e-le-fan-te'), L4 q3 ('za-pa-to'); english-short-words.ts sound-it-out q3 ('d, o, g'), short-vowels q1 ('Keep the h and the t. Put o in the middle'); english-figurative.ts idioms q3 ('counting on something'); english-figurative-es.ts idioms q3 ('¿llegar tarde o no llegar?')
findings.problem: These hints give away the answer. The pre-split syllables and the listed sounds turn the question into counting dashes or commas, and the last four hints repeat the key word or spell out the answer.
findings.fix: Hint the strategy, not the split ('Say pizza and clap each part. Count your claps.'), and paraphrase without the answer's key word ('Lin is planning for something that may not happen.').

findings.where: english-short-words.ts sound-it-out q2 ('Which word says pig?') and read-sentences q3 ('Which sentence says the cat is on a mat?')
findings.problem: The correct choice is printed word for word in the prompt, so the child can match the shapes without decoding anything. These items do not test reading.
findings.fix: Keep the target out of the prompt: 'Which word names a farm animal that says oink?' (pig/big/peg); 'Which sentence matches: a cat sits on a rug you wipe your feet on?'

findings.where: english-rhymes-syllables-es.ts:236; english-parts-of-speech-es.ts:63,176,285,392-393; english-figurative-es.ts:158,282,375; also figurative-es idioms sorter category 'Estar distraído', personification-hyperbole q3 'rechinaba'
findings.problem: The sorter instructions say 'Ordena…'. Spanish worksheets use 'Ordena las palabras' to mean 'unscramble into a sentence', and the app's own sorter text says 'clasificar' (w.sort.readout 'clasificadas'). The grade 2 title 'Ordena las palabras' over a sentence is especially misleading. The category 'Estar distraído' breaks the pattern of 'Es muy fácil / Cuesta muchísimo'. For wooden stairs, 'crujía' is the natural verb; 'rechinar' is used more for hinges and metal.
findings.fix: Use 'Clasifica cada palabra/oración', 'Clasifica por sílabas', 'Está distraído', and 'crujía'.

findings.where: english-figurative-es.ts idioms s4 sorter item 'ser coser y cantar'
findings.problem: The saying is mostly used in Spain, is never introduced in the slides, and comes with no context, so most Latin American 4th graders can only get it by elimination.
findings.fix: Introduce it in s1 with a 'en España se dice…' note, or replace it with 'ser un juego de niños'.

findings.where: english-parts-of-speech.ts adjectives s1 ('How many: three cats') vs sentence-parts q1 explanation ('The other two sentences have no adjective')
findings.problem: The course uses traditional school grammar (number words are adjectives), and that same tradition also counts a/an/the as adjectives. A parent taught that way would say 'The tree sways.' has an adjective, so the key looks wrong to them.
findings.fix: Use article-free choices ('Tall trees sway.' / 'Trees sway.' / 'Birds sing.') or drop the 'How many' line.

findings.where: english-fact-opinion.ts main-idea-purpose s2 (Text A)
findings.problem: 'the densest fur of any animal: no other animal has so many hairs…'. Guinness and NOAA-style sources say 'of any mammal', and say otters stay warm through fur plus a high metabolism. The claim is right in substance, but the wording goes past the sources.
findings.fix: 'They have the densest fur of any mammal, up to about a million hairs per square inch.' Optionally add 'and a fast-burning body'.

findings.where: `practice` exports in english-rhymes-syllables.ts, english-short-words.ts, english-parts-of-speech.ts, english-figurative.ts, english-fact-opinion.ts (re-exported by the -es files)

findings.where: english-rhymes-syllables.ts and english-rhymes-syllables-es.ts lessons what-rhymes and make-rhymes
findings.problem: The rhyme lessons go straight from spoken words to printed-word sorters, with no picture step, so a pre-reading K child can work only through the read-aloud button. The syllable lessons do the concrete, picture, number sequence well (clap, dots, number line).

eng-grammar-69.verdict: Not ready to ship as is. The 29 skills exist, the registry and tests are as described (I counted 9, 10, 8 and 12 skills in grades 6 to 9), and npx vitest run src/practice passes. My own audit script found no key that disagrees with the bank, so no hard-wrong answer reaches a child. But reading every bank entry as a teacher turned up nine major problems. In each one, either a child who picks a defensible answer is marked wrong, or a hint states the answer. Three of the author's notes were understated: the Spanish free relative "Quien termine primero" is still in g7 at level 2, filed as working like a noun (that part is defensible); "Ella" is still the name in the English dangling-modifier item (fine in English); and the curiosa item is not the only weak connotation item. Everything else the author claimed checked out. I committed nothing and deleted my scratch files; git status is clean at 3e109d2.
eng-grammar-69.sampled:
Setup: git reset --hard 3e109d2 (git log -1 shows 3e109d2) and APFS-cloned node_modules. I read all 13 bank files plus shared.ts in full: every entry, both languages. That is all of every bank (14 to 25 entries per level), more than the 25 random items asked for. I wrote a throwaway vitest audit (now deleted) that ran makeItem for every skill, every level, both locales and 320 seeds, about 50,000 items. For each item it checked:
- The key against an independent match of the item back to its bank entry.
- That check(answer, index) accepts the key and rejects every other index; that answerText returns the right label; and that check(answer, answerText(...)) as a string never passes.
- Distinct choices, the right choice present exactly once, and a kebab-case why tag on every wrong choice.
- All three hints, by whole-word search for the answer.
- say for "^", digit/digit, braces, leftover "___", " : " and run-on prompts.
- alt and visual: none in this strand.
- English words leaking into Spanish copy, and Spanish into English.
- en and es prompts and hints that are identical.
- At least 12 distinct items per level (the minimum observed was 14).

Independent recomputes:
- The Works Cited order, re-sorted with my own Intl.Collator on the first surname with accents stripped: all 28 keys match.
- MLA in-text citations, parsed from the source line: all match. The one mismatch was my own parser.
- Spanish verbals by word ending: all match.
- Spanish moods from my own list of forms: all match. This also flagged two Spanish commands that read the same as statements.

I also ran the whole practice suite (737 passing including my file), counted English skills per grade (6:9, 7:10, 8:8, 9:12), checked the CCSS codes, and fact-checked every factual claim. All were correct: the Amazon, the Pacific's share of the planet, Everest, flour weight, teen sleep hours, Pluto 2006, Marie Curie's two Nobels, Odysseus, the Apollo records, peanuts as legumes, and the four heart chambers.

findings.where: apps/web/src/practice/english/grammar-69/g7-style.ts, e.wordiness level 1, EN entry “The museum has a collection of ancient fossils from long ago.”
findings.problem: Two right answers. The key is “from long ago”, and “ancient” is tagged cut-needed-word. But cutting “ancient” leaves “The museum has a collection of fossils from long ago.”, which loses no meaning. A child who cuts “ancient” is marked wrong. Both choices always appear, because the entry has only 2 wrong choices.
findings.fix: Replace the wrong choice “ancient” with a word that is truly needed, such as “collection” or “museum”. Or rewrite the item so only one phrase is redundant, for example “ancient fossils that are very old” with only “that are very old” as the key.

findings.where: g7-style.ts, e.wordiness level 2 (WORDY_PHRASES), ask in both locales
findings.problem:
The ask is “Which word or words can replace {t} without changing the meaning?” and the Spanish says the same. Most “still-wordy” distractors also keep the meaning, so under the question as written they are correct:
- “is able to” for has the ability to
- “in advance of” for prior to
- “take into consideration”
- “reached the conclusion”
- “has a need for”
- “made an effort”
- “At this moment in time”
- “every single day of the week”
- ES “llevó a cabo una revisión de”, “efectuaron una visita a”, “dio inicio a”, “arribó a la conclusión de”
Only hint 2 says to rule out wordy choices. The older e.concision skill in upper.ts already words this correctly: “clearest and most concise, with the same meaning”.
findings.fix: Change the ask to “Which shorter, plainer word or words can replace {t} without changing the meaning?” and in Spanish “¿Qué palabra más breve y sencilla puede reemplazar {t} sin cambiar el significado?”.

findings.where: g8-verbs.ts, e.verb.moods level 1 (MOOD_NAME), EN subjunctive entries
findings.problem:
The English entries have no target, and the ask is sentence-level: “What mood is this sentence in?”. Each subjunctive sentence has an indicative main verb:
- “The coach insists that every player be on time.”
- “I wish I were taller.”
- “It is important that she arrive early.”
- “The teacher suggested that he study with a partner.”
“Indicative” is a defensible answer, since the main verb is indicative, yet it is marked wrong. The clues point to the subordinate verb (“Look at ‘be’…”), which the question never names. The Spanish level already targets the verb: “¿En qué modo está el verbo {t}?”.
findings.fix: Give every English MOOD_NAME entry a target, for example “be”, “were”, “arrive”, “study”, “would visit” and “Did… finish”. Change the English ask to “What mood is the verb {t} in?”.

findings.where: g8-verbs.ts, e.verb.moods level 2 (MOOD_FORMS), level hint 2 in both locales
findings.problem:
Hint 2 contains the answer.
- Spanish: hint 2 reads “…va el subjuntivo (quiero que vengas)… (si fuera)… (estudiaría)”. The bank items “Quiero que ___ a mi fiesta.” (key vengas) and “Si yo ___ tú, estudiaría…” (key fuera) are therefore answered word for word by the hint.
- English: hint 2 says “use ‘were’… use ‘would’ or ‘could’”, which names the key of every were/would/could item. My audit flagged 361 such item instances.
findings.fix: Use examples that are not in the bank and do not name the key form, for example “(ojalá que llueva)”, “(si tuviera tiempo)” and “(If she had a map…)”. State the rule without the target word, for example “the past form of ‘be’ used for every person” instead of “were”.

findings.where: g7-clauses.ts, e.combining.sentences level 1 (COORDINATE): “The power went out…” in EN and ES, and the bakery item in ES
findings.problem:
Some distractors are accidentally right.
- “The power went out, but we played board games by candlelight.” and “Se fue la luz, pero jugamos juegos de mesa con velas.” are natural concessive sentences: the outage could have ruined the night, but we made the best of it.
- “La panadería vende pan fresco, pero también vende panecillos.” is fully idiomatic Spanish for adding a fact. “pero también” is a standard pattern.
Children who choose these are marked wrong.
findings.fix: Use a distractor whose relationship is clearly wrong. For the outage item use “or”, for example “Se fue la luz o jugamos…”. For the bakery item use “así que”.

findings.where: g7-modifiers.ts, e.modifiers level 1 (MISPLACED): the almost/casi pizza entry, EN and ES
findings.problem: The setup is “Mia ate nearly all of the pizza. One slice was left.” The wrong choice “Mia almost ate the whole pizza.” is ordinarily read by native speakers as “ate most of it”, because “almost” scopes over “ate the whole pizza”. In Spanish, “Mía casi se comió toda la pizza” is the most natural way to say exactly this. The key is contestable in both languages.
findings.fix: Use “only”, where the placement really changes the facts. For example: setup “Mia ate pizza and nothing else”, key “Mia ate only pizza.”, distractor “Only Mia ate pizza.”, and in Spanish “Mía comió solo pizza.” / “Solo Mía comió pizza.”.

findings.where: g7-modifiers.ts, e.modifiers level 1: the tickets entry (EN and ES) and the muddy-paws puppy entry (EN)
findings.problem:
Two distractors are clear, acceptable sentences marked as misplaced.
- “Sam bought two tickets for the concert that cost five dollars each.” and “Sam compró dos boletos para el concierto de cinco dólares cada uno.”: “each” and “cada uno” can only refer to the plural tickets, so there is no misreading.
- “The puppy ran across our clean kitchen floor with muddy paws.” is a normal sentence in which “with muddy paws” describes the running.
A careful writer could produce any of these.
findings.fix: Use distractors where the misplacement produces a real wrong reading. For example, drop “each”: “two tickets for the concert that cost a lot”. Or attach the phrase to a noun it plausibly fits, for example “The puppy ran across the kitchen floor near the door with muddy paws.”.

findings.where: g6-pronouns.ts, e.vague.pronouns level 1 (AMBIGUOUS), ES “Elena le prestó a Carmen su libro de cuentos.”; the same sentence is also used at level 2 (CLEAR_REVISION)
findings.problem: The key “Cualquiera de las dos: Elena o Carmen” is contestable. You cannot lend Carmen her own book, so pragmatically “su” can only be Elena's. A native reader picks “Solo Elena” and is marked wrong. The level 2 revision builds on the same flawed premise.
findings.fix: Use a verb that works with either owner, for example “Elena le mostró a Carmen su libro de cuentos.” or “Elena le habló a Carmen de su libro de cuentos.”. Update the level 2 entry to match.

findings.where: g9-sentences.ts, e.semicolon.colon level 2 (COLONS), ES letter-greeting entries: “Querida abuela…”, “Estimado señor Díaz…”, “Querido Tomás…”
findings.problem: The item gives no context (shown is ""), so nothing says the words are a letter salutation. The options “Querida abuela, te escribo desde el campamento.”, “Estimado señor Díaz, le escribo para pedirle información.” and “Querido Tomás, gracias por tu carta.” are then correctly punctuated sentences with a vocative. They are marked wrong (comma-after-greeting). The RAE colon rule applies only to the salutation of a letter.
findings.fix: Put context in shown, for example “El saludo y la primera línea de una carta:”, as the English formal-style items do with “A sentence for…”. Ideally also show the salutation on its own line.

findings.where: g8-verbs.ts, e.verb.moods level 1, ES “Apaga la luz al salir.” and “Escucha con atención las instrucciones.”
findings.problem: The tú command form is identical to the third-person present indicative, and nothing marks either sentence as a command. “(Ella) apaga la luz al salir” is a grammatical statement, so “Indicativo” is defensible. “Cierra la puerta, por favor” and “Siéntate” avoid this problem.
findings.fix: Add a vocative or “por favor”, for example “Leo, apaga la luz al salir.” and “Escucha con atención las instrucciones, por favor.”. Exclamation marks are banned by the strand test.

findings.where: g8-pauses-shifts.ts, e.ellipsis.dash level 2 (OMISSIONS), EN and ES
findings.problem:
Several keys teach that it is fine to cut attribution or hedging from a quotation:
- “The volcano, scientists believe, is unlikely…” becomes “The volcano … is unlikely…”
- “The new park, the mayor said on Tuesday, …”
- “The test, according to Ms. Kim, …”
- the Spanish “según los científicos”, “dijo la alcaldesa”, “según la maestra Kim”
Each cut turns a reported belief into a bare assertion, which is exactly the kind of distortion the hint says to avoid.
findings.fix: Replace those asides with purely descriptive ones, such as “built in 1910” or “covered in snow”. Or make the cut attribution a wrong choice tagged changed-meaning.

findings.where: g6-pronouns.ts e.intensive.pronouns level 2 (ES); g8-verbs.ts e.verbals level 2 (ES)
findings.problem:
Both Spanish category levels can be answered from word form alone.
- e.intensive.pronouns: every target “mismo/a/os/as” is Enfático and every clitic (se, me, te, nos) is Reflexivo, and hint 2 states exactly that rule.
- e.verbals: hint 2 maps infinitivo to sustantivo, participio to adjetivo and gerundio to adverbio, and every item follows it, so level 2 repeats level 1.
findings.fix: Add reflexive items whose target includes “mismo”, such as “se miró a sí misma” with target “sí misma”. Drop the surface rule from hint 2. Add verbal items that break the one-to-one mapping, or merge the two Spanish levels.

findings.where: g9-argument.ts, e.counterclaims level 1 (ARGUMENT_ROLES)
findings.problem: All 6 passages present their sentences in the same order: claim, evidence, counterclaim, rebuttal. The quoted sentence's position gives the answer. The 24 entries are only 6 passages.
findings.fix: Vary the order: claim last, counterclaim first, or rebuttal before evidence. Add more passages.

findings.where: g7-clauses.ts, e.phrases.clauses level 1, ES
findings.problem: The main clause of a complex sentence is labeled “Oración independiente” in “todos salieron corriendo”, “no habrá clases” and “nadamos en el lago”. Spanish school grammar calls it the “oración (proposición) principal”; “independiente” refers to coordinated or juxtaposed clauses. A Spanish teacher would object to the label, though not to the idea.
findings.fix: Rename the Spanish category to “Oración principal o independiente”, or use “Puede ir sola”.

findings.where: g6-pronouns.ts, e.vague.pronouns level 3 (SHIFTS)
findings.problem:
Two problems.
1. 8 of the 14 Spanish items test subject-verb agreement, not pronoun shifts (L.6.1c): la gente ayudó, cada uno presentó, uno mejora or duerme, puedo, tuvimos, viajó, buscaban.
2. Several possessive distractors are grammatical sentences with a different owner: “El equipo celebró nuestro triunfo”, “Los músicos… miran a tu director”, “The scientists published our results”, “My friends and I packed their bags”.
findings.fix: Swap the verb-agreement items for pronoun-shift items, for example “uno… se” against “te”, or “cuando uno… su” against “tu”. Choose possessive distractors that cannot have another owner, or add “own” or “propio”.

findings.where: shared.ts build(): say for e.greek.latin.roots level 1 and e.analogies level 1
findings.problem: The shown word runs straight into the question with no punctuation, as in “geography What does the root “geo” mean in this word?”. The analogy pairs are read as “finger : hand How are these two words related?”, where TTS may say “colon” and has no pause.
findings.fix: Join shown and ask with “. ” when shown lacks end punctuation. Write analogy pairs as “finger and hand” in say, or use a dedicated say field.

findings.where: g6-vocabulary.ts ROOT_WORDS inaudible (EN and ES); g6-asides-spelling.ts CONFUSED_2 savia (ES); g9-evidence-mla.ts IN_TEXT Chen (EN)
findings.problem:
Several diagnostic tags are wrong, so the learner model records the wrong misconception.
- inaudible: “able to be heard” is tagged meaning-of-other-part, but it is ignoring “in-”, which the header defines as opposite-root. “very loud” is tagged opposite-root but is guessed-from-topic.
- savia: “sabía” is tagged sound-alike-wrong-meaning, but its stress differs from savia/sabia. The sabia item tags the same word extra-accent.
- Chen: “(Chen, page 7)” is tagged page-abbreviation.
findings.fix: Swap the two inaudible tags in both languages. Tag “sabía” extra-accent in the savia item. Tag “(Chen, page 7)” comma-in-citation, or add a page-word tag.

findings.where: Spanish wording: g9-sentences.ts semicolon level 1 #1; g9-clauses-tone.ts purpose #6; g7-style.ts analogies level 2; g6-vocabulary.ts roots level 1
findings.problem:
Some Spanish reads unnaturally.
- “El autobús llegó tarde; perdimos el primer timbre” is a calque, not natural Spanish.
- “robar la piña más grande del jardín”: in Mexican Spanish, which the rest of the strand uses, “piña” means pineapple.
- “renacuajo… charco”: a “charco” is a puddle; tadpoles live in a “charca” or “estanque”.
- The roots clue “pedestre” means vulgar or ordinary to most speakers.
- The root target “scri” in “manuscrito” is not a cited root form.
findings.fix: Use “llegamos después del timbre”, “la piña de pino más grande” or “la bellota más grande”, “estanque”, “peatón”, and target “manu” (mano) or “scrib/script”.

findings.where: g6-vocabulary.ts, e.connotation level 1 (ES)
findings.problem:
Two items weaken the positive / neutral / negative design the English items keep.
- The curiosa item has no neutral option: “preguntona” and “entrometida” are both negative.
- In the entrometido item, “inquisitivo” is tagged opposite-connotation, but in Spanish it often carries a suspicious or prying sense (“mirada inquisitiva”), so it is nearly right.
findings.fix: Use a neutral option such as “preguntadora” or “interesada” in the curiosa item. Replace “inquisitivo” with “interesado”.

findings.where: g8-verbs.ts, e.verb.moods level 2 (EN)
findings.problem:
Two English keys rest on a usage that is not universal:
- “Kai talks as if he is the boss” (tagged indicative-for-subjunctive) is widely accepted in standard English.
- “recommends that Ana drinks” and “suggest that he leaves” are standard in British English.
The keys are fine for US grade 8, but these distractors are defensible.
findings.fix: Make the contrary-to-fact meaning explicit, for example “Kai is not the boss, but he talks as if he ___ the boss”. Or use distractors that are unambiguously wrong, such as “will be” or “drank”.

findings.where: Level hints: e.analogies level 2 hint 1; e.confused.words level 1 hint 2
findings.problem:
A hint contains the answer word by coincidence.
- For “Hot is to cold as tall is to ___” (key: short), hint 1 says “in a short sentence”.
- For the than/then item (key: then), hint 2 says “…, then pick the spelling”.
This breaks rule 4 literally, and it can cue an alert child.
findings.fix: Use “in a few words” and “…, and pick the spelling”.

findings.where: apps/web/src/practice/answer.ts, used by every choice skill including all 29 here
findings.problem: For choice answers, check(answer, answerText(answer, choices)) returns false. answerText returns the label, while check compares the response to the numeric index. The Runner and tools.ts pass the index, so learners are graded correctly today. But any caller that round-trips answerText, such as “show me” or a future API, would mark the key wrong.
findings.fix: Have check accept either the index or the exact label for choice answers. Or document that choice responses must be indices and add a test for it.

findings.where: g7-style.ts, e.wordiness level 1: EN “The end result was a tie game.” and ES “Las hojas volaban por el aire con el viento.”
findings.problem:
Two items are borderline.
- Cutting the wrong choice “result” leaves “The end was a tie game.”, which is grammatical and keeps nearly the same meaning.
- “volar por el aire” is a widely accepted expression, so it is a weak example of redundancy.
findings.fix: Offer “tie” and “game” as the wrong choices in the first item. Replace the second with a clear Spanish pleonasm, such as “subir arriba”, “salir afuera” or “lo vi con mis propios ojos”.

findings.where: g8-pauses-shifts.ts e.ellipsis.dash; g9-sentences.ts e.semicolon.colon (standard field)
findings.problem: Each skill carries one CCSS code, but its level 2 teaches a different standard. Omissions with an ellipsis are L.8.2b, not L.8.2a. Colons are L.9-10.2b, not L.9-10.2a.
findings.fix: If the schema allows only one code, use the stem (L.8.2, L.9-10.2) or the code of the dominant level. Otherwise list both.

findings.where: apps/web/src/catalogue/science-water-cycle-es.ts:263 (lesson around-the-cycle, s1)
findings.problem: "Aguanieve: gotas de lluvia que se congelan en bolitas de hielo al caer por aire frío" gives the US meaning of "sleet" (ice pellets). In Spanish, aguanieve means rain mixed with snow (RAE: "agua que cae de las nubes mezclada con nieve"), so the Spanish course teaches a wrong definition of a real word.

findings.where: science-life-cycles.ts:48-58 and science-life-cycles-es.ts:48-58 (lesson every-life-cycle, s3)
findings.problem: Under the heading "Fast and slow life cycles" and the line "Some life cycles go around quickly", the first example is "An adult mayfly may live only a single day". A grade 3 child will read this as a one-day mayfly life cycle, but a mayfly's cycle usually takes about a year, almost all of it as an underwater nymph. The other bullets (dog 10-13 years, tortoise, bristlecone) are also lifespans, not cycle lengths, so the slide mixes up the two ideas.
findings.fix: Retitle the slide "Short lives and long lives", or make the mayfly line accurate: "A mayfly lives about a year, mostly underwater as a nymph. The winged adult may live only a day." If a truly fast cycle is wanted, a fruit fly goes from egg to adult in about 10 days.

findings.where: science-life-cycles.ts:324 and :365 (lesson frogs-and-more, s4 and s6 q2 hint); science-life-cycles-es.ts:327 and :368
findings.problem: "A baby has the same body shape as a grown-up, only smaller" (es: "Un bebé tiene la forma de un adulto, pero en pequeño") is false. A newborn's head is about 1/4 of its length against about 1/8 for an adult, and its limbs are relatively short. The hint "same body shape as the grown-up" repeats the claim.
findings.fix: Say "A baby has the same body parts as a grown-up. It does not change into a new kind of body" (es: "Un bebé tiene las mismas partes del cuerpo que un adulto"), and make the hint say "same body parts".

findings.where: science-life-cycles.ts:24 and science-life-cycles-es.ts:24 (lesson every-life-cycle, s1)
findings.problem: The life cycle is defined as running "from birth until it has young of its own", but the next slide teaches four parts that include death. The two definitions contradict each other.
findings.fix: Use one definition: "A life cycle is the set of changes in a living thing's life, from birth to death. Its young start the cycle again."

findings.where: science-life-cycles-es.ts:271, :285, :358 ("Rana joven") vs apps/web/src/practice/science/early.ts s.life.cycles bank ("Ranita (renacuajo con patas)")

findings.where: science-water-cycle.ts:24 and -es.ts:24 (lesson three-states, s1, particles alt)
findings.problem: The ice alt text says "Particles packed tightly in neat rows, all touching". The drawn circles have gaps (r 9 on a 22 grid), and for water in particular ice is less tightly packed than liquid, which is why it floats. Screen-reader users get a description that differs from the picture and plants a misconception.

findings.where: science-atoms.ts lesson inside-atom s3 sorter, items 'element' and 'isotope'
findings.problem: The sorter grades two facts that lesson 1 never teaches. 'Its number decides which element the atom is' (Proton) is first taught in atomic-number s1. 'Adding one makes a heavier version of the same element' (Neutron) is first taught in atomic-number s4 (isotopes). The neutron clue is also ambiguous: adding an electron also adds mass and leaves the element unchanged (it makes an ion), so 'Electron' is a defensible answer that gets marked wrong.
findings.fix: Move both items into the atomic-number lesson (e.g., add them to the s5 sorter, or a new sorter after s4). Alternatively, add to inside-atom s1: 'The number of protons decides which element an atom is. Atoms of one element can have different numbers of neutrons.' Either way, reword the clue to 'Adding one to the nucleus makes a heavier version of the same element'.

findings.where: science-atoms.ts lesson periodic-table s4 sorter (boron, neon, sodium, aluminum)
findings.problem: The sorter asks the child to sort elements the lesson hasn't sorted. The course never mentions boron, and with no periodic table shown, a child cannot work out that boron is a metalloid. Neon is first described in s5, after the sorter. Sodium and aluminum are named in lesson 2 but never called metals before this point. A child who reasoned correctly from the slides still gets marked wrong.
findings.fix: In s3 change the metalloid point to 'Boron and silicon are metalloids. Silicon is used in computer chips.' Either move the s5 'Families' slide before the sorter, or make the item self-contained: 'Neon, a gas that glows in signs'. Optionally add 'Sodium and aluminum are metals' to the metals point.

findings.where: science-weather-climate.ts lesson water-in-air s3 'From cloud to precipitation', Hail bullet
findings.problem: Wrong fact. The slide says strong rising winds 'carry them up through the cloud again and again'. NOAA NSSL calls the repeated up-and-down cycle a textbook myth. Hailstones grow while the updraft holds them up and supercooled droplets freeze onto them. Their layers come from changing temperature and water conditions as they drift sideways across the updraft, not from repeated trips.
findings.fix: Replace with: 'Hail: lumps of ice that grow inside thunderstorms. Strong rising winds hold them up while tiny supercooled droplets freeze onto them, layer by layer, until they are too heavy and fall.'

findings.where: science-cells.ts and science-cells-es.ts (all 4 lessons)
