Cell size is taught only as a list of numbers, and the only concrete model (the cell in a bag) comes at the end of lesson 2. The author's notes imply every course has visuals. Part of this is a platform gap: there is no visual kind for a cell diagram.
findings.fix: Add a number-line visual to made-of-cells s4 (EN and ES), e.g. {kind:'number-line', min:0, max:100, marks:[0,25,50,75,100], marker:8}, with alt text along the lines of 'A line from 0 to 100 micrometers. A dot at 8 marks a red blood cell; a human egg cell would reach the end, at about 100.' Consider opening cell-parts with a concrete comparison before the list of parts (the factory picture the s.cells bank already uses). Separately, raise the missing cell-diagram visual kind with product.

findings.where: Hints in science-weather-climate.ts weather-now s6 q1; science-ecosystems(-es).ts roles s5 q1 and q2; science-atoms.ts inside-atom s4 q1 and periodic-table s6 q2
findings.problem: These hints give the answer away instead of helping the child reason. 'Its name starts with “baro”' picks Barometer. 'Which one is a kind of algae?' picks Seaweed. 'It eats both plant parts and animals' restates the definition of omnivore. 'Electrons are in the cloud around the nucleus' rules out both wrong choices. eng-reading-69.verdict: Not ready to ship. I found no wrong answer keys: every key is right or defensible, and all mechanical checks pass. There are still six major problems. (1) Lengthening 117 wrong choices made the key almost always the second-longest choice. Always picking the second-longest choice scores 60–100% in 6 of 8 skills, against 25% by chance. (2) Theme-statement items follow one template and can be solved about 85% of the time without reading the passage. (3) On about 14 items, hint 3 quotes the very sentence the key paraphrases. (4) The Apollo 13 and polio passages are built the same way but keyed to different structures, so each has two defensible answers. (5) The night-market summary key gets a fact wrong (friends instead of cousins). (6) The free-buses passage presents Kansas City's fare-free buses as current, but fares returned on June 1, 2026. Smaller problems: doubled curly quotes in three English hints, structure hints that name the answer, two story inconsistencies, one poem biology error, misapplied tags, a few Spanish wording issues, and the tutor tool's 80-character limit. The author's claims hold on these points: 45 passages, 12–19 questions per skill per level, the 'la estrofa' fix, stanza locating in paired texts, and the Benin Bronzes count (about 1,130, joint declaration of July 1, 2022).
eng-reading-69.sampled: Reset to e0ee818 and copied in node_modules. The author's tests pass (558: reading-69.test.ts plus skills.test.ts), and eslint and tsc are clean for the strand. I read every passage and every question in English and Spanish: 45 passages, 215 authored questions and 10 overall-structure questions. That is all of them, more than the 25 per skill asked for. I read them as a teacher and as a native Spanish speaker, checking facts, ambiguity, distractors, hints and natural Spanish. The throwaway vitest audits, now deleted, built 400 seeds × 8 skills × 2 levels × 2 locales (12,800 items). For each item they: found the key again from the prompt text alone (no mismatches); checked that check() accepts only the key's index and that answerText returns the key label; checked choices are distinct after normalizing, the key appears once, and every wrong choice has a tag; checked hints against the key with accents and punctuation stripped; checked say for notation and newlines; checked there is no visual or alt text and that seconds are 60–240; checked every pool entry is reachable (12–19 per skill per level, all reached); checked Spanish is never just English; and checked Spanish typography. They also simulated learners who never read the passage (longest, second-longest, shortest, a theme template rule, mirror pairs), counted structure signal words with my own word lists, measured word overlap between hint evidence and the key, and dumped hint 3 and step 1 for 450 distinct items. Web checks: Kansas City fares returned June 1, 2026 (KCUR); about 1,130 Benin Bronzes in the July 1, 2022 Germany–Nigeria declaration; Tallinn transit is still free for residents; no Cedar Hollow found in New York. All scratch files and audit tests are deleted, and the worktree is clean at e0ee818. Nothing was committed.

Its length rank is 2 of 4 in 13/13 central.summary L2 questions (en and es), 12/12 pov L2 en, 14/16 theme L2 en and 15/17 words L2 es. Over 400 seeds, always picking the second-longest choice scores: central.summary L2 100% en and es (L1 78%/86%), author.pov L2 100% en and 83% es, word.choice L2 92%/93%, theme L1 es 92% and L2 86%/81%, inference L1 78%/72% and L2 es 83%, text.structure L2 en 75%, argument L2 en 71%. findings.where: All 15 theme.statement questions (L1: night-market, second-chair, fourth-street, low-tide, the-map, river-keeps, grandmother-hands; L2: interpreter, radio-hands, rumor-snowball, ninety-first, perfect-picture, snow-day, night-shift, two-tongues), en and es
findings.problem: Every theme-statement item has the same four shapes: a 1–2 word topic, a plot retelling with character names, a sweeping claim, and a key that hedges with 'can' or 'deserve'. In 11 of 15, the sweeping claim uses always, never, should, every or cannot. Hint 2 even says 'Rule out single words, retellings of the plot…'. findings.where: apps/web/src/practice/english/reading-69.ts itemFor (hint 3 = quoted ? ruleOut : reread). Items: start-later argument.evidence (L1, en/es), library-saturdays argument.evidence, argument.reasoning and pov.view (L1), middle-recess argument.evidence and pov.response (L1), science-fair compare.agree (L1), monarch-relay compare.agree (L1 en), alligator-crocodile structure.section (L1), comets-asteroids infer.what (L2 en), clock-debate argument.evidence and compare.agree (L2), wall-opens compare.agree (L2)
findings.problem: The generator only avoids pointing at the evidence when the key is an exact quote. When the key paraphrases the evidence sentence, hint 3 reads that sentence out. Examples: middle-recess, key 'The CDC recommends at least sixty minutes…', hint 3 'Reread paragraph 2: “The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends … sixty minutes…”'. start-later, key 'A school that starts at 9:00 won a basketball championship', hint 3 'Reread paragraph 3: “their basketball team won the state championship last year.”' library-saturdays reasoning, key 'The claim that only someone who has never been inside a library…', hint 3 quotes that very sentence. findings.where: passages-69/l2-info.ts apollo-13 structure (key problem-solution) and polio-vaccine structure (key chronological); e.text.structure L2, en/es
findings.problem: Both passages have two defensible answers to 'How is the passage mainly organized?', and they are keyed against each other. res-ela-sci.verdict: PASS with minor fixes. There are no blockers or major findings. All 72 added links (50 url and 22 urlEs) return 200 with no redirects. Each lands on the page its title promises. All are free with no sign-up and come from reputable sources. Every urlEs page is really in Spanish, and so are the three Spanish-only books. All 50 entries' skill fits exist on the skill map, and the resources tests, eslint and tsc are clean. The commit counts check out: 25+25 entries, "10 with Spanish" (7 urlEs plus 3 Spanish-only books) and "16 with Spanish" (15 urlEs plus the NPS Spanish booklet). These commits add links only, no answer keys. What is left is small: one legacy Java sim that repeats a sim already listed, one third-party Spanish page with a number mistranslation, two descriptions that overstate or need a caution, Spanish-only books showing for English learners on topic searches, nine fits that never match on practice pages, and two edition or grade-band tweaks. Process note: the session's working directory was the main checkout on branch foundation, not a dedicated worktree. So I did not run `git reset --hard` there. I audited from a detached worktree at 584ecbf in the scratchpad and removed it afterwards, along with all my scratch files. Nothing was committed, and the main repo is untouched (HEAD d8d8166, clean).
res-ela-sci.sampled: I checked all 72 added URLs with a browser user agent, using both GET and HEAD. The 72 are 50 url, 14 explicit urlEs, and 8 Spanish PhET links built by the phet() helper. LibriVox: language, readers and author dates for 6 pages. Standard Ebooks: the read-online links. PhET: HTML5 or legacy for each sim, and that the Spanish build file exists for the 7 HTML5 sims. Also checked the Zoo listing (221 animals) and one Zoo fact page, the Ask A Biologist cell viewer, NOAA's food-web and cloud text, and the LOC Kids/Teens/Adults lists. sci-69.verdict: The computed answer keys are sound, but the strand should not ship as is. 1 blocker and 12 major issues remain. I re-derived every computed key from the prompt text alone, with my own parsers, for 10 computed skills × 2 levels × 400 seeds. Methods: atom balancing by brute force and a separate parser, exact BigInt decimals for scientific notation, my own unit table, and two astronomy models for the Moon (Meeus ch.49 true phases, accurate to under 1 minute on the 2024–26 eclipses, and low-precision lunar longitudes). I found no wrong keys, and English and Spanish always show the same numbers. All 34 USNO moon references are real and fall between 11:00 and 23:00 UT. 8,000 moon items were in the keyed 45° phase sector at every US local noon. The checker accepts every key and rejects every wrong choice and every listed wrong value. The blocker is a bank question whose marked-wrong choice is the literally correct answer (heat.transfer, identical shirts). The major issues: a computed item that says an object "moves at 0 m/s"; hints that lead to the wrong number or state false facts (balancing); level-wide hint 2 that states the answer for about 45 bank entries; a test-wise length cue (the right answer is the longest choice in 51% of bank entries vs about 27% by chance); one DNA distractor that is accidentally right; Spanish agreement errors in generated templates; and two Spanish wordings that change the science. Nothing was committed; the scratch audit files are deleted.
sci-69.sampled: Setup: git reset --hard 4c36ba71a (HEAD 4c36ba7), node_modules cloned, the author's upper-more.test.ts passes (82 tests). I wrote throwaway vitest audit files (since deleted) that import SCIENCE_6_9_MORE and SCIENCE_6_9_MORE_BANKS. (1) Generic checks: all 34 skills × every level × 400 seeds × en/es. I checked: check() accepts the key and rejects every wrong index and every listed wrong value; typed variants (commas, unicode minus) are accepted; choices are distinct; the right choice appears once with no why tag; every wrong choice has a kebab-case why; hints and alt text vs the answer; say notation (^, digit/digit, braces, plus arrows and subscripts); Spanish present and different from English; same key in both languages; English words leaking into Spanish and the reverse; template leaks; "1 + plural"; at least 12 distinct items per level (smallest: 13 for banks, 40 for wave.speed L2). (2) Independent recomputation of every computed key from the prompt text: graph.rates, population.growth, energy.ke.pe, sci.notation, wave.speed, ohms.law, momentum, half.life, balance.equations, percent.composition. 400 seeds × 2 levels each, plus a check that en and es carry the same numbers. (3) Moon: Meeus ch.49 phases cross-checked against a low-precision elongation model (worst gap 0.25°) and 5 known eclipse instants; all 34 MOON_EVENTS verified; 8,000 items checked across every US local hour of the target date. (4) Balancing hint text checked against the full equation for 6,000 seeds per level. Length-cue and answer-position statistics for all 358 bank entries. A 3,000-seed Spanish grep for agreement slips. (5) Read as a teacher and a native Spanish speaker: every bank entry in all 7 bank files (358 entries, both languages, about 4,000 lines), all of moon/data/notation/physics/chem.ts, and a 25-seed en+es dump per computed skill per level.

findings.where: apps/web/src/practice/science/upper-more/g6-earth.ts:410, HEAT_TRANSFER, s.heat.transfer L1, en+es
findings.problem: The stem reads "Two identical shirts lie in direct sunlight. Which one warms up faster?" (es: "Dos camisetas iguales..."), but nowhere says one is black and one is white. Taken literally, two identical shirts warm at the same rate. That is exactly the choice marked wrong ("Both warm up at the same rate", tag ignores-surface-color), while the key is "The black shirt". findings.where: apps/web/src/practice/science/upper-more/physics.ts:371, momentumItem, s.momentum L1 (lab cart)
findings.problem: If the cart mass has tenths (1.5, 2.5, 3.5, 4.5 kg) and v10 is drawn as 5–9, then `v10 -= v10 % 10` rounds the speed to 0. The item then reads "A lab cart with a mass of 4.5 kg moves at 0 m/s. What is the momentum?" with key 0. Seen at seeds 104578, 455185 and 1051832 (about 1.4% of L1 items). Separately, p = 1 renders as "1 kilograms metro por segundo" / "1 kilogram meters per second".

findings.where: apps/web/src/practice/science/upper-more/chem.ts:288, balanceItem hint 3, s.balance.equations L1
findings.problem: Hint 3 gives the other side's atom count and leaves out atoms of the same element already on this side, so it points to a wrong number. Cases found: 6 CO₂ + 6 H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + __ O₂ (hint: 18 O on the left, each O₂ has 2, suggests 9, key 6); the reverse respiration equation (9 vs 6); C₂H₅OH + __ O₂ (3.5 vs 3); 2 H₂O₂ → 2 H₂O + __ O₂ (2 vs 1); 2 SO₂ + __ O₂ (3 vs 1); 2 NO + __ O₂ (2 vs 1); Ca or Na + H₂O → … + __ H₂ (2 vs 1); 2 NaHCO₃ → … + __ CO₂ (3 vs 1).
findings.fix: When sameRest > 0, say it: "The left side has 18 O atoms; 6 are already in C₆H₁₂O₆ on the right, so O₂ must supply 12. Each O₂ has 2." (the steps already compute this). Or prefer an element whose sameRest is 0 when one exists.

findings.where: apps/web/src/practice/science/upper-more/chem.ts:289, balanceItem hint 3, s.balance.equations L2
findings.problem: Hint 3 says "Start with an element that appears in only one substance on each side, such as O", which is false in at least 16 equation and formula cases. Examples: CH₄/C₂H₆/C₃H₈/C₂H₅OH/glucose combustion (O is in CO₂ and H₂O), photosynthesis, 2 SO₂ + O₂ → 2 SO₃, 2 NO + O₂ → 2 NO₂, Fe₂O₃ + 3 CO, Ca or Na + H₂O (H is in two products), NaHCO₃, CaCO₃ + HCl. A hint that states a false fact teaches the wrong strategy.
findings.fix: Choose el only from elements that really appear in exactly one substance on each side (if none exists, say to balance the others first and leave this one for last), or drop the claim and keep "Each F has n X atoms".

findings.where: Bank `strategy` (hint 2, shared by every entry of a level): g6-life.ts ORG_THEORY/ORG_PARTS/BODY_JOBS, g6-earth.ts ROCK_CYCLE, g7-banks.ts PHOTO_IO/MIXTURES/REACTION_SIGNS, g8-life.ts GEOLOGIC_TIME, g8-physical.ts CLIMATE_IMPACT/WAVES_INFO, g9-matter.ts BONDING/NUCLEAR, g9-systems.ts DNA_PROTEIN/CARRYING_CAPACITY/EARTH_ENERGY
findings.problem: The level-wide hint 2 is a glossary that states the answer outright for about 45 entries, against the rule that no hint contains the final answer. Examples: geologic.time "Earth is about 4.5 billion years old … dinosaurs died out about 66 million years ago … life began at least 3.5 billion years ago" answers entries #0, #2 and #8 verbatim. findings.fix: Rewrite each bank strategy as a method ("name the job first, then think which part does that job") and move the facts into per-entry clue and explain. findings.where: All 26 bank levels (SCIENCE_6_9_MORE_BANKS); worst are s.climate.impact 12/13, s.nuclear 11/14, s.resources 10/13, s.claim.evidence 9/13, s.waves.info 9/14, s.design.criteria 9/16
findings.problem: Length cue: the correct choice is strictly the longest in 183 of 358 entries (51%), where chance is about 96 (27%). A test-wise learner who always picks the longest option scores 92% on climate impact and 79% on nuclear without knowing the science. That makes mastery data from these drafts unreliable.
findings.fix: Edit the distractors to roughly the key's length and detail, or trim the qualifiers from keys ("The lithosphere, which is broken into plates" → "The lithosphere"). Add a test that limits how often the key is strictly longest (for example ≤35% per bank).

findings.where: apps/web/src/practice/science/upper-more/g9-systems.ts:51, DNA_PROTEIN entry #4 ("One strand of DNA reads A T G C")
findings.problem: The distractor "G C A T" (tag base-pair-mixup) is the reverse complement, which is how the partner strand reads in its own 5'→3' direction. A grade-9 student who knows strands are antiparallel can defend it as correct. Also, the clue (hint 3) "Pair each base in order: A with T, T with A, G with C, C with G" spells out the key letter by letter.
findings.fix: Replace G C A T with a real pairing error that is not the reverse complement, such as "C G T A" (A↔C, T↔G mix-up). Optionally say "read in the same direction". Change the clue to the rule only ("A pairs with T and C pairs with G; pair each base in order").

sci-k5.verdict: I found no wrong answer key. All 9 computed skills matched my own recomputation on 552,000 generated items, and every hand-written key in the banks is factually right. It is still not ready for 1.0: 3 major problems and 15 minor ones need fixing first. Majors: (1) the climate data tells children Canada and the northern US have average July highs of 80–95°F (Canada: 65% of items say above 85°F, which no Canadian city has); (2) one grade-1 light question has two defensible answers and marks the true one wrong; (3) grade-5 material identification (level 3) has only 6 distinct questions, so they repeat. Most serious minors: "unas 1"-type Spanish grammar errors in about 26% of Earth's-water level 2–3 Spanish items; every water-wave scenario describes waves that could not exist; hint 2 (the level-wide hint) restates the answer on about 25 recall questions; picture and answer-length patterns let children guess right. The authors' claims hold up where checked: daylight hours match a sunrise–sunset calculation, the gas from the fizzing cup stays within what baking soda and vinegar can make, desert towns get under 10 inches of rain, and the existing tests pass (207 for this strand, 904 across practice). I committed nothing and deleted my scratch files; the worktree is clean at 2d5827e.
sci-k5.sampled:
Setup: worktree reset to 2d5827e; node_modules copied as clones (left in place, ignored by git). Throwaway audit script covering all 33 skills, every level, both locales; it ran once with 600 seeds and once with 4,000 seeds (552,000 items).
(1) For every computed skill I worked out the key myself from the prompt text and picture data, never from the generator's own variables: weather tallies, daylight against a sunrise–sunset model for Denver, Philadelphia, Columbus and Indianapolis, habitat counts, climate, motion, waves read from the graph points, mass and stoichiometry, a material table I wrote myself, and Earth's water shares. 0 mismatches.
(2) check() accepted every key and rejected every wrong choice and every listed wrong value; number-line answers always fall on the line. 0 failures.
(3) Choices: no duplicates, key appears exactly once, every wrong choice has a kebab-case tag, the key has none. 0 failures.
(4) Hints: flagged 48 hint kinds containing the answer word or number; reviewed each by hand.
(5) Read-aloud text: no ^, digit/digit, braces, blanks or math symbols. 0 failures.
(6) Spanish is never just English (only "Alaska" is the same in both).
(7) Alt text: reviewed 18 flags.
(8) Every bank level has 13–14 distinct items.
Extra probes: test-taking cues (picture on the key, key as the longest choice); counts of Spanish "unas 1"; whether the iron hint ever helps; water-wave steepness; how often Canada July temperatures are unrealistic.
Manual reading: every bank entry (about 600 across all 46 bank levels) in English and Spanish, plus 2 seeds of every computed level in both languages, read as a teacher and as a Spanish reader. Also compared the NGSS codes with the first strand (early.ts), and ran the existing strand tests (207 pass) and all practice tests (904 pass).

findings.where: apps/web/src/practice/science/k5-more/computed-3-4.ts:17-20 (NORTH/SOUTH ranges), s.climate.data L1+L2, en+es
findings.problem: The data presented as fact is wrong. Canada and the northern US get average July highs drawn from 80–95°F (3,000 seeds: 63% of northern items state July above 85°F; Canada 493/761 = 65%). Real July average highs: Toronto 81, Montreal 79, Ottawa 80, Winnipeg 79, Vancouver 72, Calgary 74, Minneapolis 83, Chicago 84, Boston 82. April up to 68 and October up to 70 are too warm for Canada too. Australia's July range of 50–60 is too cold for Sydney (63), Perth (65) and Brisbane (71). Keys are still right, but the child is told false climate facts. The strand test only checks the ordering of the temperatures.
findings.fix: Use realistic ranges that keep the order. North: Jan [15,40], Apr [48,62], Jul [72,84], Oct [50,62]. Australia: name Melbourne/Adelaide, or use Jul [55,64] with Apr/Oct minimums above 64. Better: per-place tables from NOAA/ECCC/BOM normals, plus a test that each stated value falls inside the place's real range.

The key is 'No light gets through', but the wrong choice 'The light bounces back' is also true: a book reflects light diffusely, which is how you see the lit spot. A child who says that is marked wrong and tagged thinks-it-reflects, which is not a misconception. Item 4 (clear water, 'bounces back') has a milder version of the same problem.
findings.fix: Replace that wrong choice with one that is plainly false (e.g. 'The light shines out the back of the book'), or reword the stem to 'Does any light come out the other side?'

findings.where: apps/web/src/practice/science/k5-more/computed-3-4.ts:306 (wave-tank context) and :394 (compareWaves), s.wave.shape L1-L3
findings.problem: Every water-wave scenario is physically impossible. eng-phonics.verdict: Not ready to ship. Every answer key I recomputed independently came out right: letters, sounds, blends, swaps, sound counts, -ed/-ing and participle/gerund forms, syllable splits (checked against Merriam-Webster and my own RAE syllabifier), stress, aguda/llana/esdrújula, syllable types and compounds. The mechanical invariants also pass (check() accepts the key index and rejects the others, choices are distinct, why tags are present, no notation in say, both locales present, at least 12 items per level), and the author's 169 tests pass. Three problems should block release: (1) the English "hand" item shows a Spanish hint that is also factually wrong; (2) about 20 "Which word is spelled right?" items offer another correctly spelled real word, so there are two defensible answers; (3) the feet item uses a single-foot picture with "foot" as a distractor, and "be", "tre" and "sno" read aloud exactly as bee, tree and snow. There are also many structural problems: gap items whose distractors sound the same as the key while the hint claims they would sound different, hints that contain or spell the answer, two false Spanish spelling rules, misleading syllable hints, and vulgar Spanish words ("pito", "güevo").
eng-phonics.sampled: Reset to 2923a82 and ran the author's tests (169 pass). Wrote throwaway tsx scripts in the scratchpad, ran them, then deleted them; nothing was committed and the worktree is clean. (a) Generated items for all 28 skills, 52 levels, en and es, 300 seeds each (31,200 items). On each I checked: check() with the key index (accepted) and every other index (rejected); answerText; distinct labels with the key exactly once; why tag on every wrong choice and none on the key; hints non-empty and not containing the key; say free of notation; EN differs from ES and no language leakage; alt does not contain the key; at least 12 distinct items per level. (b) Recomputed every bank entry (about 827 entries x 2 locales) by my own rules: phoneme tables for first/last sound, vowel patterns, onset+rime and syllable joins, letter-swap rebuilds, hand-coded sound counts, gap rebuild from the spoken word, an -ed sound classifier, my own -ed/-ing spelling rules, participle and gerund tables, ES seseo phoneme rules for soft c/g, an RAE syllabifier, hand-coded MW splits, stress lists and an English syllable-type classifier. Every key matched. (c) Read every bank entry in source, both languages (all items, not only 25 per skill), plus a full render of all composed hints and steps. (d) Checked in Runner.tsx and AnswerPad.tsx how picture, alt, hints and choices render: alt is only an aria-label, hints are shown as text and have their own Hear button.

findings.where: grade1c.ts:76-79 EN_VT_READ (e.vowel.teams L2 EN)
findings.problem: Picture-word items have distractors that are right or decode exactly to the picture's name. The feet item uses 🦶, which is a single FOOT (its Unicode name), and offers "foot" as the wrong choice, so the distractor names the picture better than the key. The bee item offers "be", tree offers "tre" and snow offers "sno": all three decode by open-syllable rules to exactly bee, tree and snow, so a child who decodes correctly is marked wrong.
findings.fix: Feet: use a 'shoe' or 'sheep' style item or change the distractor to fat:V. Replace be, tre and sno with distractors that sound different (bed, try, snap); keep homophone spellings only in items explicitly asking for the correct spelling.

findings.where: read.ts:112 gapQ hint 3; data grade1c.ts:59-66 (e.vowel.teams L1 EN, all 16), grade2a.ts:21-27 (e.r.controlled L1 EN: bird, girl, shirt, turtle, purse, burger, tiger, spider), grade2a.ts:61-67 (e.diphthongs L1 EN, all 16), grade1b.ts:26-28 (whale/w, duck and sock with k/c), grade2a.ts:69-75 (e.diphthongs L1 ES ei/ey)
findings.problem: The task is "Which letters are missing?" for a word that is spoken aloud, but at least one wrong fill sounds identical (ai/ay, ee/ea, oa/ow, ir/ur/er, oi/oy, ou/ow, wh/w, ck/k/c, ei/ey), so the item has two phonetically valid answers. Hint 3 then claims the homophone sounds different: "With ay, it would say rayn", "With ur, it would say burd", "With oy, it would say coyn", "With ea, it would say feat", "With ow, it would say howse", "Con ei diría rei". The EN diphthong hint 2 even admits "oi and oy sound alike" but gives no rule for choosing.
findings.fix: Ask "Which spelling is right?" for these items and teach the position rule in hint 2 (ay/oy/ow usually end a word; ai/oi/ou come in the middle). For homophone-tagged fills, hint 3 should say "sounds the same, but X is not spelled that way". Alternatively, drop homophone fills from the listening gap level.

findings.where: yvowel.ts:96-100 (e.y.vowel L2 ES, all 16 items)
findings.problem: On a "¿Cuál está bien escrita?" item, hint 3 writes out the correct spelling: "Buey termina con el sonido de i.", "En aire, el sonido de i está dentro de la palabra.", "En playa, después de la y viene una vocal". Hint 2 also spells rey and reina, which are themselves items. The hint gives the answer every time.
findings.fix: Use 'la palabra' instead of w in hint 3 ("Esta palabra termina con el sonido de i"), and use examples in hint 2 that are not in the bank (hoy → ley is in the bank too; use 'convoy', 'peine').

findings.where: endings.ts:108 and :189; grade2a.ts:171; grade2a.ts:128-129 with ES_SOFT :111,:113,:114; grade2c.ts:74
findings.problem: Hint 2 contains the exact answer on these items: participio hint lists escrito, roto, hecho (escribir, romper and hacer items); gerundio hint lists durmiendo and leyendo (dormir and leer items); silent letters hint shows "knot, lamb" (knot and lamb items); soft c/g ES anchors "como en sol" and "como en jirafa" are the key on cereza, gente and genio; syllable split examples "rab-bit" and "pe-lo-ta" are the rabbit and pelota items.
findings.fix: Choose worked examples outside the bank (dicho, vuelto; pidiendo, cayendo; knee, comb; seta/zapato; nap-kin, ca-mi-sa), or skip the example when it equals the key.

findings.where: letters.ts:55 (e.letter.names L1 EN, all 16 items)
findings.problem: The task is to hear a letter name and find its shape, and the prompt deliberately shows no glyph. Hint 3, which is displayed as text, says "N looks close, but it is not M." This puts the target glyph on screen, so a pre-reader can simply match shapes. The Spanish version correctly uses the letter name ("no es la eme").
findings.fix: Name the letter in the English hint ("N looks close, but it is not em") or point only at the look-alike ("N looks close. Listen again.").

findings.where: yvowel.ts:107 (e.y.vowel L2 ES hint 2) and grade2a.ts:90 (e.diphthongs L1 ES hint 2)
findings.problem: Both hints teach a false Spanish spelling rule. "El sonido de i al final se escribe y" and "Al final de la palabra, la i se escribe y" would make a child write casy, aquy, fuy, my, jabaly. The y applies only to an unstressed i closing a diphthong (rey, hoy, muy). The grade2a hint is also shown on the au/eu items (auto, pausa, euro, dinosaurio, astronauta, aplauso), where it does not apply.
findings.fix: "Al final, la i que va después de otra vocal y no lleva tilde se escribe y: rey, hoy, muy (pero: casi, fui, leí)." Give the au/eu items their own hint.

findings.where: grade2c.ts:122 (e.syllable.types L1 EN: me, she, we)
findings.problem: Hint 2 says "Open ends in a vowel. Silent e ends in e." The key-open items me, she and we end in e, so the hint supports both 'open' and 'silent e'.
findings.fix: "Silent e: vowel, one consonant, then an e you do not hear (cake). Open: the word ends with the vowel sound (go, me)."

findings.where: grade2c.ts:75 (e.syllable.split L2 ES: río, sandía, país)
findings.problem: Hint 2 "No se separan ... diptongos como io o ue" points to the wrong choice on río ("io": key rí-o, distractor río) and does the same on sandía and país. These are hiatuses because of the tilde.
findings.fix: Add: "pero si la i o la u lleva tilde, se separan: rí-o, pa-ís, san-dí-a".

findings.where: read.ts:46 MISS['dropped-letter'] with grade1c.ts:75-80 (e.vowel.teams L2 EN, all 16) and grade2a.ts:77-82 (e.diphthongs L2 EN: coin, point, house, cloud, mouth, noise)
findings.problem: Hint 3 says "X is missing a sound" for distractors that drop a letter of the vowel team but keep the same number of sounds (ran, tran, snal, shep, fet, lef, sel, pech, bot, got, sop, rod, bol, con, pint, hose, clod, moth, nose). Be, tre and sno even sound the same as the key. The statement is false.
findings.fix: For vowel-team drops, use 'has one vowel where two belong' (a new tag such as 'single-vowel-for-team'), or change the dropped-letter text to 'is missing a letter'.

findings.where: sounds.ts:112 (e.word.families L1 ES, -ito); blend.ts:79 (e.blend.onset L2 ES, pa+to); grade1c.ts:23 (e.silent.e L1 ES, huevo); grade1a.ts:23,41 (e.short.vowels L1 ES, pato)
findings.problem: Age-inappropriate Spanish. "pito" (common vulgar slang for penis in Spain, Mexico and Argentina) is spoken aloud by TTS ("Gatito, perrito, pito.") and shown as a choice. "güevo" (vulgar in Venezuela, Colombia and the Caribbean) is a distractor. Hint 3 on the pato item reads "Con po diría poto" (buttocks in Chile and Peru).
findings.fix: Use palito/bonito/grito for -ito and pita/pino for pa+to; replace güevo with uebo; reorder the pato distractors so hint 3 uses pe ("pe-to" is also odd, so use ba → "bato").

findings.where: sounds.ts:29 (e.middle.vowel L1 ES, bici)
findings.problem: In a listening item, boca is tagged matched-consonants and hint 3 says "Boca tiene las consonantes de bici". By sound that is false: bici is /bisi/ and boca is /boka/.
findings.fix: Use 'beso' (b-s, vowels e-o) as the near miss, or tag it different-vowel.

findings.where: grade2a.ts:128 and :143, ES_SOFT and ES_SOFT_READ (e.soft.c.g ES)
findings.problem: The items assume seseo: cereza starts like sol, "Con e, i, la c suena como en sol", and zereza/sereza "suena igual". This is false for Castilian Spanish, where ce, ci and z are /θ/.
findings.fix: Declare Latin American Spanish as the target in the content or the UI, or word the hint as "en casi toda América suena como en sol".

findings.where: grade2a.ts:122 (e.soft.c.g L1), endings.ts:42 (e.ending.ed L1 EN), yvowel.ts:25 (e.y.vowel L1 EN), letters.ts:151 (e.final.sound ES)
findings.problem: The written prompt can be met by the written labels, which leads to the misconception being taught. "Read: city. Which picture starts the same?" — the label 'cat' starts with the same letter. "Which word ends like jumped?" — all three choices end in -ed. "ends like fly" — both cry and baby end in y. In ES, "¿Cuál termina como gato?" with key perro is read as a final-syllable rhyme in Spanish classrooms.
findings.fix: Say "starts/ends with the same sound" in the prompt itself, as the say line already does.

findings.where: yvowel.ts:43 (yoyó), :66-69 (my, yes), :32 (hint 2 anchors)
findings.problem: Some keys repeat the word being asked about. "¿Cómo suena la y en yoyó?" has key "como en yoyó"; "y in my" has key "i, as in my"; "y in yes" has key "y, as in yes". Hint 2's anchors ("In fly... In baby...") equal the key on the cry, butterfly and daisy items.
findings.fix: Use anchors that are not bank words ("como en yema" → use "como en llave"; "i, as in kite"; "y, as in yo-yo") and pick different hint anchors.

findings.where: read.ts:89, sounds.ts:159, core.ts:38 altFor (all picture-word reading levels plus e.word.families L2)
findings.problem: The alt text (the picture's aria-label) is the key itself ("A cat" on "Which word names the picture?"), so a screen-reader user hears the answer. Sighted children are not affected.
findings.fix: For reading-the-picture items, use a neutral alt ("Picture to name" / "Dibujo para nombrar") or describe the picture without its name.

findings.where: apps/web/src/practice/answer.ts check() and answerText() for kind 'choice'
findings.problem: check(answer, answerText(answer)) rejects the key on every choice item: answerText returns a string (the index, or the label when choices are passed), while check compares it with === to the numeric index. Runner and tools.ts pass the index, so this is latent today, but any caller that uses answerText output will mark right answers wrong.
findings.fix: In check, accept Number(response) === index or a label match, or document that choice answers take the index.

findings.where: sight.ts:183 (algodón), grade2a.ts:47 (corro) and :49 (encerrar), grade2b.ts:84 (houseboat), grade1b.ts:42 (cherry/berry)
findings.problem: Some distractors are defensible answers. "¿Hay algodón en la puerta?" is a sensible sentence. "El corro canta" works, since corro is a ring of children. "El perro quiere encerrar su hueso" is sensible. A houseboat is arguably 'a kind of house'. A 🍒 is often called a berry by children.
findings.fix: Replace these with clearly nonsensical look-alikes (alguien → alfombra is also sensible, so use 'algodonero' → better 'alguno'; corro → 'cono'; encerrar → 'enterado'; houseboat → swap the one-part option to 'a kind of boat'? no — that is the key's head; use a different compound; berry → 'chewy').

findings.where: endings.ts:109 (e.ending.ed L2 ES, salir)
findings.problem: Hint 3 says "Salado no va después de he." This is false: "he salado" is correct Spanish (from salar). It is wrong only as the participle of salir.
findings.fix: "Salado viene de salar, no de salir." Or use 'salaído'-style non-words such as 'saldo'? Better: 'salado' → replace with 'saliado'.

findings.where: grade2b.ts:115 and :114, grade2b.ts:38
findings.problem: The Spanish compound hints sound unnatural: "Un girasol hace algo con sol.", "Un paraguas hace algo con aguas.", "La segunda, sobre qué lo hace." Also, "alto" is tagged one-part-only for alta+voz but is neither part.
findings.fix: "La segunda palabra dice con qué: girasol → sol." Use 'alta' or 'voz' as the one-part distractor.

findings.where: sight.ts:87 (e.sight.preprimer L2 ES: tu/tú, se/sé)
findings.problem: The tilde diacrítica (tu vs tú, se vs sé) is tested in the pre-primer band, which is kindergarten. It is normally taught in grades 2-3, so the item is age-inappropriate for this band.
findings.fix: Move these items to the grade 2 band and replace them here with non-accent look-alikes (te, tos, su).

findings.where: blend.ts:38 (e.blend.onset L1 EN rimes an/up/at/all) and blend.ts:175 (e.sound.swap L2 EN "Change the a in hat to i")
findings.problem: Speech engines reduce function words. "Then add an." comes out as /ən/; "Then add up." sounds like the phrase 'add up'; "the a in hat" comes out as a schwa. The child hears the wrong sound.
findings.fix: Quote the parts and name letters explicitly (add the ending "an"; 'the letter a') or use rimes that are content words (ox, ice, oat, eat).

findings.where: grade2a.ts:152 and :129 (e.soft.c.g)
findings.problem: The ES hint "Se escribe ce, ci, ge, gi..." points to the wrong choices girafa and tigeras on the jirafa and tijeras items. The EN hint "Before e, i, or y, g often says j" sits next to keys gift and girl (hard g before i) on the gum, goat and gold items.
findings.fix: ES: add "el sonido de jirafa también se escribe ja, je, ji, jo, ju". EN: pick anchor keys that follow the rule (gum → gate, goat → gas).

findings.where: endings.ts:159 (e.ending.ing L2 ES, poder)
findings.problem: "Estoy pudiendo" (poder in the progressive) is unnatural Spanish for a child's model sentence.
findings.fix: Replace with vestir → vistiendo or elegir → eligiendo.
